en: [Page 1] // Commentary on the Five Aggregates (Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā) //
Homage to the Buddha! The treatise begins with the words "The five aggregates," and so forth.
Its purpose is for the sake of explaining the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena (*dharma*).

Now, one might object: since the characteristics of phenomena have already been definitively established in treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, is not further effort toward their determination redundant?
It is not redundant, because it serves the needs of disciples who possess ready understanding (*udghaṭitajña*).

For those with ready understanding are capable of comprehending, by means of a mere indication, all the specific details that may arise from it without exception; thus, they hold the concise statement itself in high regard, rather than an extensive exposition.
Therefore, this treatise has been commenced for the sake of favoring those beings who take delight in concise presentations.

Alternatively, because householders are occupied with many duties, it is impossible for them to apply themselves to extensive texts; and even for renunciants who are devoted to mental cultivation, application to extensive texts leads only to distraction. Thus, for the sake of both groups' understanding of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), the characteristics of phenomena are presented here in this treatise.
Since it has been stated in brief, there is no pointlessness in undertaking this work.

Alternatively, those who have mastered the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) through this summary will be capable of understanding the detailed exposition of the characteristics of phenomena without effort; therefore, the Master composed this treatise as an introductory gateway to the extensive texts such as the *Yogācārabhūmi*.

Furthermore, why is it that without an understanding of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), [the goal] is not accomplished—such that the Master takes such care in the exposition of the characteristics of phenomena?
It is for the sake of one-pointedness of mind (*cittaikāgratā*) during the definitive resolution of discussions, and for skill in answering questions.
For indeed, when one has cultivated familiarity with the characteristics of phenomena, the mind becomes one-pointed upon an object as desired due to the absence of doubt; it is not otherwise.
Furthermore, through the discernment of the characteristics of phenomena and by attaining the excellence of wisdom, one acquires fearlessness;
being fearless, one becomes capable in the definitive resolutions of discussion regarding all questions and their explanations, and not otherwise.

"Five aggregates" is a determination of number by way of precluding both deficiency and excess. Because the term "aggregate" is used without qualification, it includes both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) aggregates.
There are exactly five aggregates, neither fewer nor more.
This is for the purpose of demonstrating the objects grasped as "self" and "belonging to self.
For generally, among the foolish, the grasping of a self occurs with respect to consciousness alone,
while the grasping of what belongs to self occurs with respect to the remaining factors, such as form and so forth.
For instance, the grasping at a self in the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) consists in the notion that the self is related to external and internal form as its instrument or its object.
The grasping at a self in the aggregate of feeling (*vedanāskandha*) consists in the notion that the self experiences feeling, which is the maturation of pure and impure karmas.
In that regard, the maturation of wholesome karmas is a pleasant experience;
that of unwholesome karmas is painful;
and that of both is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
In this context, from the perspective of ultimate reality, only the equanimity associated with the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is the maturation of karma,
because the storehouse consciousness itself is the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karma.
As for pleasure and pain, however, they are metaphorically designated as "maturation" because they are produced from maturation.

The aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is the grasping at "mine" because, through the medium of perception, the conventional usage of the self proceeds with respect to objects seen, heard, thought, and known.

The aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is the grasping at "mine" because, by means of wholesome, unwholesome, and other formations, there is the impelling of the mind—which is regarded as the self. Thus, there are exactly five aggregates.
Now, why is the sequence of the aggregates exactly as it is?
It is according to their degree of grossness (*audārikata*).

Among them, form (*rūpa*) is the grossest of all because it possesses resistance (*sapratighatva*), because it serves as the basis for the five groups of consciousness (*pañcavijñānakāya*), and because it is the object of the six consciousnesses.
Therefore, gross matter was mentioned first.
Feeling is grosser than the other three because its activity is grosser;

for even though it does not occupy a location like perception and the others, because its activity is grosser, people designate it by means of a spatial delimitation, saying, "I have a feeling in my hand," or "I have a feeling in my head," whereas they do not do so for perception and the rest.
Therefore, it is mentioned immediately after form (*rūpa*).
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is coarser than those two because it is easily characterized by its nature of grasping signs (*nimitta*).
Volitional formations (*saṃskāra*) are coarser than consciousness (*vijñāna*) because they are easily understood through their characteristic of conditioning.
Because it is the most subtle of all, consciousness is mentioned last of all.

The term "rūpaskandha" (form-aggregate) would have to be either a coordinate compound (*samānādhikaraṇa*) or a genitive determinative compound (*ṣaṣṭhī-tatpuruṣa*); it cannot be a coordinate compound.
Because the aggregate lacks substantial reality;
since the word "aggregate" (skandha) is a synonym for "heap," therefore the aggregates exist as designations, like a heap.
Consequently, there would be an absence of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).
Furthermore, even a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound would not be possible;
for a relationship exists only between two things that possess mutually distinct forms.
It would be like [the expression] "Devadatta’s maternal uncle.
Furthermore, this genitive case used for the sake of indicating a relationship—as in "of the aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandhayoḥ*)—implies that the aggregate is something other than form;
yet this is not accepted.
There is no such fault, because that which exists as a conceptual designation (prajñaptisat) cannot be described as being either identical to or different from its own constituent basis (upādāna).

Even in cases of non-difference, the use of the genitive case is observed, as is its use for things that cannot be described as identical to or different from [their basis], such as "the body of the statue."
Regarding the "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva) of form:
for an image is not other than the body;
and since prior non-existence is likewise indefinable, it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from it.

Because identity and difference are based on intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), that which is grasped and designated in dependence upon the apprehension of another entity is a conceptual existence (*prajñaptisat*), since it lacks an intrinsic nature distinct from its material cause (*upādāna*). And in this very way, the referent of the aggregates (*skandha*) is said to be a conceptual existence.
And therefore, even though it cannot be described as being either identical to or different from its own material cause (*upādāna*), the use of the genitive case is not contradictory;
consequently, in this instance, it is indeed a genitive *tatpuruṣa* compound.
What is form?
It consists of the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements.
But is this not an irrelevant question, since the aggregates (skandhas) were the subject under discussion when it was asked, "What is form"?
It is not unrelated,

because since the aggregates lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it is impossible to determine [the person] by means of designating their intrinsic nature; rather, it is determined solely by means of designating their appropriation (*upādāna*).
Therefore, the question is "What is form? and not "What is the aggregate of form?
In order to demonstrate the distinction between form by way of its causal relationship, he says: "The four great elements," and so forth.
For indeed, all the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are the cause of all derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*),
and all derived matter is the effect of all the great elements.
The greatness of the elements is due to their coarseness, insofar as they serve as the basis for all derived matter.

Alternatively, their "greatness" (mahattva) arises because they exist as a great configuration within all collections of form and so forth, due to the presence of solidity and the other [characteristics].
Furthermore, their "element-ness" (bhūtatva) means that they are called *bhūta* because they come into being (*bhavanti*) in various ways during the production of the diverse forms derived from them.
Or, they are called *bhūta* because, through the sovereign power of the karma of all sentient beings, they have never at any time not existed throughout beginningless saṃsāra.
Nor does it follow that other things would be [realities], because they are conventional terms (*rūḍhi-śabda*) like "buffalo" and so forth.
Furthermore, these are exactly four, neither fewer nor more, because otherwise there would be the consequence of incapacity or meaninglessness.
For the function of the derivative [matter] consists solely in supporting, cohesion, maturation,
and expansion; since its purpose is fully accomplished by these alone and there is nothing else to be done,
there are exactly four primary elements.

But surely, like support (*dhṛti*) and so forth, providing space (*avakāśa*) is also an effect of derived form (*upādāyarūpa*), and since that is produced by space (*ākāśa*), it follows as a consequence that space, like earth and the other elements, would be a great element (*mahābhūta*). This is not so.
What is the reason?
For there is no such thing as "space" other than the mere absence of resistant matter;
and it is only a resistant object that, within its own space, makes room for another resistant object by withdrawing from it.
Nor is it space;
for it is not logical that space withdraws from that location like a material object, such that it would grant room [to another].
Furthermore, matter, being characterized by resistance (*sapratigha*), obstructs the arising of other matter in its own location.
It is not space.

Therefore, when there is an absence of space for something in a certain place while that [other thing] exists, and when that [other thing] is absent, there is space for it in that place; thus, by that very [thing] moving away from that spot, space is granted to it.
"Not by space" means that,
therefore, space is not a great element like earth and the others.

Regarding the phrase "derived from the four great elements" (*catvāri ca mahābhūtāny upādāya*), both instances—"the four great elements are form" and "form derived from the four great elements"—are connected by the word *ca* ("and"). In five ways—as the causes for production, reliance, support, maintenance, and nourishment—the great elements take hold of the derivative matter (*bhautika*); thus, the term *upādāya* has the sense of a cause.
For example, it is understood that fire exists by depending on fuel; thus, it is by way of that cause.
In this context, [the elements] are the cause of production because without them there is no arising of derived matter.
They are the cause of support because when the primary elements undergo transformation, the derived matter supported by them conforms to that transformation.

The primary elements (*bhūta*) function as the cause of stability because they serve as the cause for the non-interruption of a similar continuum even for derived matter (*bhautika*). They function as the cause of support because [derived matter] does not cease by virtue of them.
They function as the cause of growth because, when the primary elements increase, the derived matter that depends upon them also increases.

The explanation beginning with "the earth element" (*pṛthivīdhātu*) and so forth is as follows: because they maintain their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), earth and the others are indeed "elements" (*dhātu*).
The mention of "earth and the others" is for the purpose of distinguishing them from the eye element (*cakṣurdhātu*) and so forth, as well as from one another.
The mention of "element" is for the purpose of differentiating them from worldly earth and the like.
For earth and the other elements are asserted to be twofold according to the distinction between worldly convention and the established tenets of the treatises.
Among these, the worldly ones—consisting of color and shape—are merely conventional and thus not [ultimate] elements (*dhātu*).
The scriptural ones, however, because they possess the intrinsic nature of hardness and so forth, are ultimate and therefore the true elements.
Since even the earth element and the others, like [the aggregates], are not understood without a definition of their own nature, there is another question: "What is the earth element? and so forth.

In the term *khakkhaṭatva*, the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). Solidity itself is "solidity" (*khakkhaṭatva*); for there is no other entity here besides solidity.
"Hard," "rough," and "harsh" are synonyms.
"Moisture" refers to the water element; it is called moisture because its nature is cohesion or because of its fluidity.
Because of its burning quality, heat is the fire element.
"The wind element is lightness and motion.
If it were said that "lightness" is the wind element, it would follow that even derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) would possess the status of a primary element (*bhūta*).

If it were said that "motion" is the wind element, only its activity (*karman*) would be indicated, not its intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*). Therefore, in order to distinguish it from lightness—which is a derived matter—and from activity, [it is defined] in this way.
It has been stated that the wind element is lightness and mobility (*laghusamudīraṇatva*).
Furthermore, mobility is the state of being the cause for the continuous arising of the stream of entities in different locations.
How is it known that these elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—exist inseparably from one another, just as they do with derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)?
By way of their function;
for this very reason, their activities are said to be supporting, gathering, maturing, and expanding.
How indeed [is it that these are established], even though they are not perceived by way of their own intrinsic nature?
One might infer the existence of [the other elements] in stones and so forth by way of their effects.
For instance, in stones and the like, the coexistence of water, fire, and wind with the earth element is known through cohesion, ripening, and support;
in water, the coexistence of earth, fire, and wind with the water element is known through the supporting of wood, the ripening of leaves, warmth, and movement.
In fire, the association of earth, water, and air is known from the stability, cohesion, and propulsion of flames and so forth;
and in wind, the association of earth, water, and fire is known from its supporting power, its drying of clothes and such, and its non-dispersal.
What, then, is the distinction between action (*karman*) and intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*)?
Action is established in dependence upon that which is being acted upon.
For instance, the function of the earth element is said to be "support" in dependence upon its supporting the substances to be supported;
the function of water is "cohesion" in dependence upon that which is to be cohered.
The function of fire is digestion with respect to maturation; the function of wind is expansion with respect to the embryo in its stages of *kalala* and *aṅkura*, which are to be increased by karma.
Expansion, moreover, consists of growth and spreading.
However, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is independent of all other conditions; this is the distinction between function and intrinsic nature.
The elements have been explained by way of their general and specific designations, as well as by way of their intrinsic nature.

Since derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), which was mentioned immediately after the primary elements (*bhūta*), is not understood in terms of its classifications and its essential nature, he therefore asks: "What is derived matter?
The meaning is: of how many kinds is it, and what is its essential nature?
What is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the eye faculty (*cakṣurindriya*)?

"Clear form whose object is color" (*varṇaviṣayo rūpaprasāda*) is the disclosure of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). "Derived from the four great elements" (*catvāri mahābhūtāny upādāya*) is connected [to this] because it is the subject under discussion.
Color (*varṇa*) is of four kinds, such as blue, yellow, and so forth.

Alternatively, because it has color as its object—either due to the observation of color or because it is the uncommon cause for the appearance of color—it is called "having color as its object" (*varṇaviṣaya*).

This is the meaning of "clarity" (*prasāda*) here: for example, when a reflection is perceived in a clear mirror or a vessel of water, a reflected image (*pratibimba*) arises based on that [original] form.

In the same way, with respect to the five [faculties] consisting of translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*), such as the eye and so forth, cognitions (*vijñapti*) bearing the appearance of those [objects] arise in dependence upon visible forms, odors, and so on.
Here, one must effect a distinction between the eye and the other [faculties] from one another, from the object which consists of matter, from the mind (*manas*), and from faith (*śraddhā*).

Because there is no difference in their consisting of translucent matter and no difference in their having color as their object, both are described as "translucent matter that has color as its object."
In this context, it distinguishes [the eye] from the ear and other [senses] by virtue of having color as its object and by being the clarity of the object;
for neither the ear and so forth nor the clarity of the object has color as its domain.
It distinguishes it from the mind by its nature as the clarity of form (*rūpa*).
For even though that [faith] has color as its object, it does not consist of the clarity (*prasāda*) of form.
The mention of "form" serves to distinguish it from the clarity that consists of faith.
For faith also consists of clarity and has form and so forth as its objects; therefore, the mention of "form" is made.

If it were stated that "the faculty of the eye is clarity whose object is color," it would follow that faith (*śraddhā*) is also included; therefore, the term "form" (*rūpa*) is employed, because faith does not have form as its intrinsic nature.
For the eyes and so forth are called "faculties" (*indriya*) because they exercise power (*indanti*);
the meaning is that they exert sovereignty (*ādhipatya*), that is, they exercise dominance over this aggregate.
Therefore, the meaning of "faculty" (*indriya*) is the sense of sovereignty; they are called faculties because they exercise power (*indanti*).
In this way, the form *indrāṇī* would follow.
The term *indriya* will be established here by means of irregular derivation (*nipātana*). Even so, the root-meaning must still be stated;
and since that has not been stated, this constitutes the rebuttal.
It would be exactly like the case of "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

Just as, although the term *vijñāna* is derived from the sense that "it cognizes" (*vijānāti*), the suffix *-ana* (lyuṭ) is disregarded and it is called "consciousness" for the purpose of excluding the notion of a cognizer distinct from it, so too here, it would have been stated in this way for the purpose of excluding the postulation of a logical mark (*liṅga*) distinct from the sense-faculties.

For just as a distinction between the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth, has been stated based on their mutual difference of objects—namely, "What is the visual faculty? It is the translucent matter whose object is color-form (varṇa-rūpa). What is the auditory faculty?"—so too [is it here].
"Sound is the object, the translucent form [of the sense organ] is [the subject]," and so forth;
in this way, the distinction between the objects such as form and the subjects such as the eye is stated.
Form is the object of the eye alone.
It does not apply to the ear and the other [senses], because they are established as having sound and so forth as their respective objects.
And in this case, there is neither an injunction nor a prohibition regarding the mind, because it is not the subject under discussion.
In this way, the mutual distinction between form and the other [sensory objects] is stated: the object of the eye is form alone, not non-form.
Likewise, the non-difference of blue, yellow, and so forth—which are mutually distinct yet objects of the visual faculty—is stated by their common nature as form.

If it is argued that form (*rūpa*) is already specified by its being the object of the eye, then for what purpose is it stated that "form consists of color and shape (*varṇasaṃsthāna*) and intimation (*vijñapti*)"?
It is for the purpose of demonstrating the various classifications of form.

For, by demonstrating the distinctions among the various types of form, the doubts, misconceptions, and lack of proficiency of those who are uncertain, mistaken, or unskilled regarding them are eliminated.
Color is of four kinds:
blue, yellow, red, and white.
Why are cloud, smoke, dust, mist, shadow, glare, light, darkness, open space, and the sky not also mentioned here?
They are not mentioned because they do not constitute distinct varieties of form (*rūpa*) in the same way that color and shape do;
for clouds and the others occupy either delimited or undelimited locations.
In this regard, those [objects] whose location is delimited are included within shape itself;
those whose location is not delimited are merely specific types of color.
Since they cannot be established as distinct from color and shape, they are not mentioned separately here.
In this context, "open space" (*abhyavakāśa*) refers to a location devoid of any tangible object capable of providing resistance other than itself.
It is not that which is perceived as blue above;
rather, it is shape (*saṃsthāna*), namely: long, short, square, circular, high, low, even, and uneven.
But what, then, is this so-called "shape"? Has it not been stated that it is "long" and so forth? Even so, this very point remains unknown.
That in which cognitions such as "long" and so forth arise is the configuration (saṃsthāna) of length and so forth.
If that is the case, then configuration does not exist apart from color and the like.
What is the reason?
[Page 12] Because, when a greater mass of color and so forth extends in one direction, the cognition of "long" arises; when it is smaller, the cognition of "short";
and when it is equal in all four directions, the cognition of "round" arises.
The cognition of being circular arises when [the object] is equal on all sides; the cognition of being elongated arises when it faces a single direction;
and the cognition of being oblong arises when it faces various directions.
How, then, is this understood—that the cognition of "long" arises with respect to a collection of phonemes and so forth, and not with respect to a distinct entity called "shape"?
Because the cognition of "long" and so forth arises even through the medium of touch;
and a cognition does not arise through the medium of one sense organ regarding an object that belongs to the domain of another sense organ.
Because it would otherwise follow that the sense-faculties are useless;
for that is not sensory cognition at all,
but rather inferential cognition.
[Objection: It is like the knowledge of a flower’s color [derived] from its fragrance.
Just as fragrance is invariably concomitant with the color of a flower, but touch is not so [invariably concomitant] with shape, this comparison is unequal.

Therefore, since shapes such as long and so forth arise through the medium of both sense-faculties—just like a jar and the like—that shape is not a distinct entity from color and the other [sensory qualities].
Furthermore, because atoms are partless, it is not logical for there to be a mutual distinction among them based on forms such as length;

therefore, just as there are no atoms of blue and so forth, there are likewise no atoms of length and so forth. Consequently, it is also untenable to claim that a collection of shape-atoms constitutes a shape such as length, because atoms of shapes like length do not exist.
Nor is substance of the nature of shape, because of the existence of its near, middle, and far parts;
nor is there non-difference among those parts.

Because it is simultaneously perceived and unperceived, and because its relata are distinct, it must necessarily be distinct [from them]; otherwise, if there were no distinction, it would follow that even those things not related to it would be non-distinct.
Therefore, shape does not exist as a substantial entity at all.
Rather, length and so forth are designated based on the very phonemes and other elements as they are established in their respective ways.
Now, what is this phenomenon called "informative intimation" (*vijñapti*)?

It is the shape of the body produced by a mind that takes that [object] as its focal point, arising in dependence upon the primary elements of the body; it is called "informative intimation" because it makes known to others the mind that originates it.

And in this context, only that shape which arises from a mind taking that very [object] as its focal point is informative intimation, and not that which arises from a mind taking something else as its focal point.

Furthermore, for one who speaks in this manner, the shape of the lips and so forth is refuted because it arises from a mind that does not have those [lips] as its object; and that which arises from a prior vow is also refuted.
For even that arises from a mind that is a cause of maturation (*vipāka-hetu*) other than the mind of the vow itself; thus, it is not accepted as informative action (*vijñapti*).

In that case, if the shape called "informative" (*vijñapti*) were a single entity pervading the entire collection known as the body, then, because it is one and all-pervasive, it would be perceived in every limb, since it exists throughout the whole;
or else, it would not be a single entity, because it is established in distinct parts.
Furthermore, the established doctrine that the ten bases (*āyatana*) are composed of atoms would be contradicted.
Therefore, there is no such thing as shape (*saṃsthāna*) as a distinct substance;
and for this reason, shape is not a representation (*vijñapti*).
If it were something other than the body,
yet not its shape,
what then would it be?
It is the continuous arising of the bodily continuum in another location, caused by volition that has that [object] as its objective support.
Its being caused by volition is due to the production of the wind-element, which is the cause for the bodily continuum’s arising in another location.
And since that arising of the body in another location makes known the volition which is its own cause, it is called "informative" (*vijñapti*).
However, its state of being wholesome or unwholesome is not intrinsic;
rather, it is designated as wholesome or unwholesome because it is set in motion by a wholesome or unwholesome volition,
through the metaphorical attribution of the cause to the effect.

In this context, however, the determination of form (*rūpa*) is by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), configuration (*saṃniveśa*), and the characteristic of activity (*kriyā-lakṣaṇa*). By way of intrinsic nature, it refers to the four colors, such as blue and so forth,
because they have that as their intrinsic nature.
By way of configuration, there are ten types of shape, such as long and so forth,
because they are specific configurations of color;
by way of the characteristic of action, there is informative [matter], because it consists of vibration.
Since the eyes and other sense faculties have as their objects things that exist substantially (*dravyasat*),
and since shape and informative intimation (*vijñapti*) exist only as designations (*prajñaptisat*), they do not constitute the objective domain of the eye.
How, then, is it said that visible form (*rūpa*) is the objective domain of the eye?
For here, in accordance with worldly convention, "color" (varṇa) is intended as the object of the eye, being qualified by a specific configuration (saṃsthāna).
Thus, color is perceived by the eye as distinguished by its configuration,
not merely the configuration alone nor the color alone.
Because visual consciousness arises manifesting as color distinguished by configurations such as long and so forth,
it is well known in the world that both color and configuration are the objects of the eye.
Likewise, because one perceives a continuum of the body distinguished by its arising in different locations, it is also well known that informative intimation (*vijñapti*) is an object of the eye.

From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), however, even color (*varṇa*) is not an object of the eye, just like shape (*saṃsthāna*), because— like shape— an atom (*paramāṇu*) is not established [as a real entity], and because consciousness does not have external objects as its domain. Therefore,
it is understood that the Master has here merely followed what is well-known in the world and in the treatises.
Since sound was mentioned immediately after visible form, it is logical that its definition follows right after that; thus the question: "What is sound?
It is defined as "the object of the ear," meaning it is the object of the ear alone and not of any other sense-faculty.
For in this way, although there is no difference in their being derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*), [it is distinguished from the others].
Thus, its distinction from the objects of the other sense-faculties, such as visible form and so forth, has been stated.
Furthermore, since sound alone is the object of the ear, the non-difference of the mutually distinct varieties of sound in their status as the "sound-base" (śabdāyatana) has been stated.
To demonstrate those distinctions, he says: "caused by the great elements that are appropriated, unappropriated, or both."
In this context, "appropriated" refers to those [elements] included within the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) that are grasped by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) as their basis;
the opposite of these are "non-appropriated.
Since these [sounds] have those as their cause, they are said to have as their cause both appropriated and non-appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*).

In that regard, sound caused by appropriated great elements (*mahābhūta*) includes such things as the sounds of the hand or the voice; sound caused by non-appropriated great elements includes such things as the sounds of wind, forest trees, or rivers;
and sound caused by both types of great elements includes such things as the sound of a drum.
What is odor?
It is the object of the nose alone;
and the object of the nose is indeed odor, as explained previously.
However, by that [neutral odor], there is neither benefit nor harm to the sense faculties or the primary elements.
Furthermore, that odor is innate (*sahaja*), produced by combination (*sāṃyogika*), or produced by transformation (*pāriṇāmika*).
Among these, the innate is found in sandalwood, saffron, and the like.
That which arises from conjunction is the fragrance of incense sticks and the like; that which arises from transformation is the fragrance of ripe mangoes and the like.
"What is taste? and so forth;
it should be explained in detail as before that taste is the object of the tongue alone, and the object of the tongue is indeed taste.
The sixfold division has been stated according to the difference in their natures;
however, another division, based on the difference in their combinations, is infinite.
For here the exposition of derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is under discussion;

however, immediately after taste (*rasa*), only a portion of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) was designated as derived matter. Therefore, following the exposition of taste, there is a question with the desire to explain that portion of the tangible: "Which is the portion of the tangible?"
For the tangible is of two kinds: the primary elements (bhūta) and the matter derived from them (upādāyarūpa). And the primary elements have already been enumerated and explained.
But here, derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is the subject under discussion;
therefore, the phrase "a portion of the tangible" is connected with the question, "What is derived matter?

By the expression "the object of the body," it is specified that this is the object of the body alone and not of the eye and so forth, thereby indicating its distinction from visible form, sound, and the other [sensory objects].

Since the object of the body is indeed touch (*sparśa*), it is stated that there is no difference between the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) in terms of being touch, even though they are mutually distinct. [An objection is raised: "If it is said that the object of the body [is touch], then since the primary elements are also objects of the body, it would follow that they are derivative form (*upādāyarūpa*). To this he says: "excluding the great elements" (*mahābhūtāni sthāpayitvā*).
He says "smoothness, roughness," and so forth, in order to demonstrate that [touch] is a specific portion of the tangible.
But surely, that which is touched by the body-faculty (kāyendriya)—namely, smoothness and so forth—is called the tangible (spraṣṭavya).
And since whatever is touched by something necessarily touches that [thing] as well, it would follow that the body-faculty itself is also a tangible.
For nothing at all is ever touched by anything.
For if there were contact with their entire substance, all composite objects would have the dimensions of a single atom.
If there were contact by way of parts, it would follow that atoms possess constituent parts, and thus their status as atoms would be lost.

Therefore, when the object and the sense faculty arise in immediate proximity, the consciousness supported by them perceives the object; it is on this basis that it is metaphorically said that "the object is touched" by that [consciousness], but not that [the object is touched] by the sense faculty.
For this very reason, it is figuratively said that by the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) only the primary elements (*bhūta*) are touched,
and not the derived forms (*rūpa*) and so forth which depend upon them,
because they are not apprehended by body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*).
Furthermore, the impairment of color and other qualities in flowers and such things occurs through the impairment of their substrate, not through physical contact with the body.
[Objection: How can there be an impairment of the substrate of color and so forth when it has not been touched by the body?
This is a matter for reflection;
therefore, in this context, one must follow worldly convention alone,
not ultimate reality.
Smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) means being soft, gentle, and fit for embracing;
"smoothness" is simply the state of being smooth (*ślakṣṇa*).
As for "roughness" (*karkaśatva*): that which possesses *karka* (hardness) is "rough" (*karkaśa*).
Like *lomaśa*;
*karka* is a designation for strength;
*karkaśa* itself is the state of being harsh (*karkaśatva*).
"Rūkṣa" means harsh and unrefined;
"guru" means thick; "gurutva" is simply the state of being heavy.
That by which entities are weighed and sink down;
that by which entities do not sink down due to lightness.
The meaning is that even when the width of the hips is equal, that [part] from whose presence comfort is brought forth—
namely, the cause for the hips of the scale not to sag— is the "cold" (śīta). That which, when struck, gives rise to a desire for warmth, is "cold."
But surely, even though cold exists during the summer and autumn, there is no longing for heat;
since the longing for heat is absent,
it is determined that cold alone is what produces the longing for heat.
And thus, even its effect is indicated by those who employ technical definitions (*lākṣaṇika*) because it belongs to that same class:
hunger (*jighatsā*) is that which produces the desire for food;
thirst (*pipāsā*) is that which produces the desire for drink.
For there is no mental factor (*caitasika-dharma*) that is an object of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).
Therefore, applying the designation of the effect to the cause, they are here described as "hunger" and "thirst.
Indeed, a certain specific type of tangible object (*spraṣṭavya-viśeṣa*), predominantly consisting of the wind-element (*vāyu-dhātu*), arises within the stomach as the cause of hunger.
It is called "hunger" because it is the cause of hunger;
likewise, that which abounds in the fire element is called "thirst" because it is the cause of thirst.
There also exist other specific types of tangible objects, such as fainting, strength, and weakness.
These are not mentioned separately because they are included within these very [qualities];
fainting is not distinct from smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*),
and strength (*bala*) is not distinct from roughness (*karkaśa*) and heaviness (*gurutva*).
In this way, other specific types of tangible objects (*spraṣṭavyaviśeṣa*) should also be included as appropriate.
However, the mutual distinction between smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*) and the others arises from the difference in their substrata (*āśrayaviśeṣa*).
Smoothness occurs due to the predominance of the water element (*abdhātu*) and the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
Coarseness arises from the predominance of the earth and wind elements;
heaviness arises from the predominance of the earth and water elements;
lightness arises from the predominance of the fire and wind elements.
For this very reason, there is excessive heaviness in dead bodies; coldness due to the predominance of the water element;
and hunger due to the predominance of the wind element.
Thirst arises from the predominance of the fire element (*tejodhātu*).
In this way, regarding other derived forms (*upādāyarūpa*) as well, their mutual distinctions should be understood according to their respective bases (*āśrayaviśeṣa*), as the case may be.
However, only a mere indication has been shown here in order to avoid excessive prolixity in the text.

The question is: since nothing remains from the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) or from derived form (*upādāyarūpa*) except for non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), what is this non-informative matter?

Its definition is: it is wholesome or unwholesome form produced by informative action (*vijñapti*) or meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which is invisible and non-obstructive. In that regard, informative action is of two kinds.
There are bodily intimation and vocal intimation;
each of these, moreover, is divided into three types, according to the distinction of being wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate.
Non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) is also of three kinds: belonging to the desire realm, belonging to the form realm, and untainted (*anāsrava*).
Among these, non-informative matter of the desire realm arises from informative action that is either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, it consists of the Prātimokṣa restraint, the Bodhisattva restraint, non-restraint, and that which is distinct from them.

In that regard, the *prātimokṣa* restraint is fourfold in substance, being divided into [the vows of] a monk (*bhikṣu*), a novice (*śrāmaṇera*), a lay follower (*upāsaka*), and one who observes the fast (*upavāsastha*).
It is eightfold by name, due to the distinctions of monk, nun (*bhikṣuṇī*), and so forth.
Among these, the *prātimokṣa* restraint is the turning away from harming others in every way, together with its causes.
The bodhisattva vow (*bodhisattvasaṃvara*) is the engagement in every possible way in benefiting others through body, speech, and mind, regardless of one's own body, life, or possessions.
Non-restraint (*asaṃvara*) is the engagement in every possible way in harming others.
Engagement in benefiting or harming others only to a limited extent is neither restraint nor non-restraint.
In that regard, the discipline pertaining to the form realm and the untainted discipline are both born of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
These, in their respective order, are the discipline of dhyāna (*dhyāna-saṃvara*) and the untainted discipline (*anāsrava-saṃvara*).
Among these, the discipline of dhyāna is born of tainted meditative concentration within the four dhyānas, the threshold state (*anāgamya*), and the intermediate dhyāna (*dhyānāntara*).
The untainted restraint (*anāsrava-saṃvara*) is born from untainted meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Its nature as derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) is due to its proceeding and persisting by depending upon the primary elements (*bhūta*).
"This here" and "that there"—this very designation is its demonstration (*nidarśana*).
Because it does not exist there [in that location], it is non-demonstrable (*anidarśana*).
Resistance (*pratighāta*) is the obstruction of another's arising in one's own location;
since non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) has no location, such resistance is impossible for it, and thus it is non-resistant (*apratigha*).
For all form (rūpa) is of three kinds:
visible and resistant—namely, the object of the visual faculty;
invisible and resistant—namely, the five [faculties] beginning with the eye, and the four [objects] of sound, odor, taste, and touch.
Invisible and non-obstructive is the form belonging to the sphere of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

That, moreover, is of five kinds: that which is derived from contraction (*ābhisaṅkṣepika*), that which is derived from space (*ābhyavakāśika*), that which is derived from undertaking (*sāmādānika*), that which is derived from conceptualization (*parikalpita*), and that which is derived from mastery (*vaibhūtvika*).
However, since here the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is intended to consist of only eleven substances, it is stated that only the form derived from undertaking is invisible and non-obstructive.
It is not something else.
For what reason, then, was that not stated?
Because it is a condensed [explanation]: atoms themselves do not differ from colors such as blue and so forth.
Nor is the appearance of color anything other than the color itself, such as blue and so forth.

That which belongs to the space-abode consists of atoms alone, devoid of any other tangible objects that possess resistance. Since these are of the nature of color, they are already included here [among the visible objects] and thus are not mentioned again.
The imagined form, such as the skeleton and so forth which is a reflected image,

and the form belonging to the realm of liberation-meditators (vaibhūtika), which is the object of those practicing the meditative absorptions of liberation— these are not included here because they consist of conceptual construction (vikalpa).
For that [reflection] does not exist externally apart from its manifestation as a consciousness having that form;
and since the reflection is the manifestation of the object within consciousness itself, the reflection is not distinct from consciousness, nor is consciousness distinct from the reflection.
Therefore, it is said to be merely "derived" (*sāmādānika*).
It is nothing else.
For who like us is capable of fathoming the mental fluctuations of those whose power is so great?
Therefore, one must seek the intended meaning of the Teacher by not asserting anything [else].

This is what is meant: that which is produced from informative action (*vijñapti*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), being derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*)—whether wholesome or unwholesome—that follows after one whose mind is distracted, undistracted, or even mindless;
in the absence of a cause for its abandonment, it is called "non-informative" (*avijñapti*).
Although its intrinsic nature is material activity, it is called "non-informative" because, unlike informative action, it does not make itself known to another by means of its own originating mind.
And here, unlike the *vijñapti* (manifest action) imagined by the Vaibhāṣikas, even *avijñapti* (unmanifest action) does not exist at all, because it is not an object of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Nor, however, is there an absence of the *prātimokṣa* vows and so forth.

For instance, by that volition through which one—having first performed the ritual of ordination and so forth—undertakes a commitment and restrains body and speech from prohibited actions, a seed is deposited in the *ālayavijñāna* for the arising of future volitions of that same kind;
it is from this that, at a later time, the mindfulness of the undertaking arises: "I am abstaining from taking life and so forth."
When that [shame] has arisen, one who possesses shame does not break the training;
thus, it is said that restraint is the volition of undertaking accompanied by its continuity.
Likewise, one who has entered into meditative absorption (dhyāna) or the Path, even without non-informative matter (avijñapti), acquires a corresponding Path and a basis.
Because upon its acquisition, even when one has emerged from meditative absorption, one no longer engages in wrong speech and so forth, but engages only in right speech and so forth; therefore,
applying the designation of the effect to the cause, it is called [the *samvara*].
The eight path-factors and the meditative restraint (dhyāna-saṃvara) are established [as such].
Non-restraint (asaṃvara), moreover, is the volition of action involved in the practice of killing for those born into such families,
or the volition of undertaking such actions for those born into other families.
And there is no abandonment of non-restraint upon the departure of that volition,
because the intention to harm sentient beings has not ceased.
Thus, it is stated that non-restraint is the volition of action and the volition of undertaking, accompanied by the intention to harm sentient beings.
In this context, it is quite easy to understand that [the non-informative action] arises from informative action and meditative concentration; thus, it is not further elaborated here.

However, the state of being wholesome or unwholesome belongs to the volitions of restraint and non-restraint by their very nature, because their continuity is projected by wholesome or unwholesome volitions and because they are the fruit of wholesome or unwholesome volitions.

The meditative and uncontaminated restraints (*dhyāna-anāsrava-saṃvara*) are also wholesome because they have the meditative and uncontaminated paths as their cause and because they are the fruits of right speech and so forth.
Furthermore, they possess the nature of form (*rūpatva*) because they are the objects of body and speech; [this is stated] by applying the designation of the object to the subject.
However, its invisibility and non-obstructiveness are easy to understand.
Why, then, is this aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), which extends up to the unmanifest (*avijñapti*), called "form"?
For it was said by the Blessed One: "O monks, it is deformed (*rūpyate*); because it is deformed, it is therefore called the 'appropriated aggregate of form' (*rūpopādānaskandha*).
By what is it deformed?
"Even when touched by the contact of a hand, it is affected," and so forth.
For in the Sūtra it is said: "It is called 'form' (rūpa) because it is affected (rūpaṇāt) by the contact of a hand and so on.
But what is this "affection" (rūpaṇā) of form?
This is the production of something different from its previous state through contact with the hands and so forth;
and this is said with reference to the continuum (*santāna*),
not to a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
Because the moment (kṣaṇa) is defined by the two times of arising and perishing.

The question is: "Since the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha) was mentioned immediately after the aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha), it is now the occasion for its exposition; what, then, is feeling? The answer is: "Feeling is a threefold experience.
Experience (*anubhava*) is the direct realization of an object's own nature, which consists of pleasure, pain, or that which is free from both of these modes.
Alternatively, experience (*anubhava*) is that which experiences the true nature of an object as free from the three modes of pleasure, pain, and both;
and it is of three kinds according to its distinct natures:
pleasant, painful, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
But how, again, is it known that there is another third experience distinct from pleasure and pain? It is known both from scripture and from reasoning.
For it is said in the Sūtra: "There are three feelings."
Furthermore, it is said: "By the abandoning of pleasure and the abandoning of pain, [there remains] that which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant.
There is also a logical argument: because there is no arising of a mind devoid of feeling, and because a mind from which pleasure and pain have departed is perceived.
Regarding this, the Master Saṃghabhadra states that the experience of feeling is contact (*sparśa*).
The experience of pleasant, unpleasant, and those contacts which are neither is sensation (*vedanā*).
And so it has been said: "In dependence upon a contact conducive to pleasant sensation, a pleasant sensation arises," and so forth.
This is because [sensation] is distinguished by its being the producer of pleasant sensations and the rest.
And if the experience of an object were itself feeling (vedanā),
what would be its distinction from those [mental factors] that have the same object?
For it is on this basis that it is established that "the experience of contact is feeling."

If that is the case, then the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of perception (saṃjñā), resolve (adhimokṣa), mindfulness (smṛti), wisdom (prajñā), and so forth, should not be stated as being determined by way of their objects (ālambana), just as it is for feeling (vedanā).

Alternatively, if the distinction between perception and the others is asserted on the basis of the grasping of signs (nimitta-udgrahaṇa) and so forth with respect to a single object, why is this not accepted for feeling on the basis of its experiencing of the object?
Furthermore, the experience of contact (sparśa) would have to be conceptualized either as association (samprayoga) with that [feeling] or as its causal state.
Because it is impossible for that [mind] to have that [object] as its objective support,
there could be no association [of feeling] therein; for there is no distinction in the association of contact among all mental factors (caitta).
Nor is it the state of being a cause, because there is no distinction in the fact that contact (*sparśa*) is the cause of all mental factors (*caitta*).

Furthermore, the term "experience" (*anubhava*) is not well-known in either common usage or in the treatises as referring to either the effect or the cause; rather, it is well-known as referring to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*).
However, they think as follows: "Experience" (anubhava) is that by means of which one experiences the ripening of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Among these, the experience of wholesome karmas is pleasant as the ripening of their fruit; that of unwholesome karmas is painful.
For both [types of beings], there is neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling].
In this case, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) itself is the maturation (*vipāka*) of wholesome and unwholesome karma;
and the equanimity associated with it is, in the ultimate sense, the maturation of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
However, because pleasure and pain are born of maturation (*vipākaja*), they are metaphorically designated as "maturation.
In that context, [the phrase] "that of which the cessation is a pleasant experience," and so forth, refers to this.
As for what was stated regarding dependent origination—that "the feeling in whose arising a desire not to be separated from it arises is a pleasant feeling"—[that too is consistent with this].
How is that so?
There is no contradiction here, because in terms of actual meaning, the other [factors] are included.
The meaning is that when this [feeling] has arisen, a desire for non-separation occurs; by implication, it is said that when it has ceased, a desire for reunion also occurs.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "when this has ceased, there is a desire for reunion," it is also implied that when it has arisen, there is a desire for non-separation.

If that is so, then why is it that for ascetics who have encountered the obsession of passion against their will, when pleasure born of passion arises, a desire for separation occurs, and upon its cessation, a desire for non-reunion?
How is that so?
Because it does not arise from that very same [cause],
due to the refutation of that [position].
For those who perceive that pleasure as an obstacle to ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), both [of these] come to pass; thus, there is no contradiction.
That which is suffering is that at whose arising there is a desire for separation, and at whose cessation there is, moreover, a desire for non-union.
Separation is its eradication.

*Chanda* is desire, longing, or aspiration. Regarding the statement, "that from whose arising neither [pleasure nor pain] occurs," and so forth: because it proceeds from the accumulation of body and mind and possesses a pleasant nature, it is called a pleasant experience (*sukha-anubhava*). Consequently, upon its cessation, a longing for reunion with it arises once more.

Because it proceeds from the diminution of body and mind and by its very nature is disagreeable, painful experience is called "unpleasant"; thus, upon its arising, there arises a desire for its separation. However, that experience which proceeds from neither [body nor mind] and exists as such is the neither-painful-nor-pleasant [feeling].
It is like non-black-and-non-white karma.
For this very reason, because it proceeds without providing benefit or causing harm, there is no arising of either suffering or pleasure, as there is an absence of desire for both.
This threefold experience, moreover, becomes sixfold according to the distinction of its respective bases,
because it arises from contact with the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
Furthermore, it is divided into two types based on the aggregation of what is to be supported (*ādheya*):
namely, the bodily (*kāyika*) and the mental (*caitasika*).

In this regard, because they exist inseparably from the body and possess resistance (*sapratigha*), the faculties of the eye, ear, nose, and tongue are included within the "body" and are thus designated by the term "body. Consequently, there is the experience of contact through the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
That which arises from body-contact is called "bodily"; however, that which arises from mind-contact is called "mental," because it has the mind alone as its support.

Furthermore, through the distinction between the adverse side and its antidote, each type of experience is established in two ways: as "with worldly attachment" (*sāmiṣa*) and "free from worldly attachment" (*nirāmiṣa*), and as "based on greed" (*gredhāśrita*) and "based on renunciation" (*naiṣkramyāśrita*).
Worldly attachment (*āmiṣa*) refers to craving for one's own personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).

The personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) consists of the internal aggregates of appropriation (*upādānaskandha*). That craving which operates toward it—desiring, as it were, non-separation according to the principle of embracing a beloved only son—is "the carnal" (*āmiṣa*). Because it exists together with that [craving], it is "accompanied by the carnal" (*sāmiṣā*).

That which is dissociated from such craving and conducive to separation from it is "unworldly" (*nirāmiṣā*). The five desirable qualities of sensual pleasure are form and so forth. They are called "qualities of sensual pleasure" (*kāmaguṇāḥ*) because they are multiplied—that is, repeatedly practiced—by means of desire characterized by expectation, attachment, and longing.
Attachment to those things and longing for them is *gredha* (greed). That which is based upon it, or that which is based by means of it, is "based on greed" (*gredhāśrita*).
Renunciation (*naiṣkramya*) is detachment from sensual desires, or the path thereto.
That which is based on that, or by means of that, is "based on renunciation.

In this context, having placed detachment from the view of a self-identity (satkāya) at the forefront, there is an establishment of the "with-greed" and "without-greed" states by way of the relationship between the adverse and its antidote.
With reference to mundane detachment, there is an establishment of what is based on greed and what is based on renunciation.
But for what reason is the distinction here stated solely by way of its own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), and not by way of a distinction in its locus (*āśraya*) and so forth as is done elsewhere?
Because brevity is intended here, and because all distinctions are not separate from the own-nature itself, it is not stated by way of a distinction in locus and so forth.

Immediately following the exposition of the aggregate of feeling (vedanā-skandha), it is now the occasion for the exposition of the aggregate of perception (sañjñā-skandha); therefore, the question is asked: "What is perception?
Its definition is given as "the grasping of the signs of an object" (viṣayanimittodgrahaṇa). Here, "object" (viṣaya) refers to the focal point (ālambana).
The *nimitta* is a specific object,
the cause for establishing the objective basis (*ālambana*) such as blue, yellow, and so forth. Its apprehension (*udgrahaṇa*) is the determination of blue— namely, "this is blue."
"It is yellow"—

if this is so, then perception (saṃjñā) associated with visual consciousness and the others would not have the nature of grasping the signs of the object, because there would be no discernment of its specific qualities.
That [cognition] as well consists essentially in the apprehension of a sign (*nimitta*), and is not determinative because of its dullness;
otherwise, if the particularity had not been previously grasped, there could be no subsequent discernment such as "this is blue" or "this is yellow.
Although there is no difference in their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*), the distinction between them is to be understood by way of their basis (*āśraya*) and their object (*ālambana*).
In terms of their basis, there are six groups of perception (saṃjñākāya): perception born of eye-contact, and so on, up to perception born of mind-contact.
Furthermore, the object (ālambana) is that which possesses signs (sanimitta).
The signless is limited, extensive, and immeasurable.
And [the sphere of] nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*).
In that regard, the nature of a thing is "with signs" (*sanimitta*) by virtue of the sign (*nimitta*)—that is, the form of an object superimposed through the medium of sound.
The notion (*saṃjñā*) that this superimposed form upon that thing is "this is that sound" has a sign-possessing object (*sanimittālambanā*).
Furthermore, the signless (*animitta*) refers to the essential nature of things (*vastusvarūpa*) when it is free from superimposed aspects—namely, *nirvāṇa* and the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*).
Among these, these three are called "signless" because they lack superimposed signs, because they lack the signs of form and sensation, and because they are not distinct [in that regard].
For one who has not yet mastered the relationship between word and meaning, the perception (*saṃjñā*) occurs only with respect to the essential nature of form itself.
But it is not [the perception] of form itself.
Therefore, the perception whose object is that [form] has the signless as its objective support (*animittālambanā*).

Since the realm of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇadhātu*) also has as its intrinsic nature the subsiding of all signs of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), the perception associated with the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that takes that as its objective support also has the signless as its objective support.
The Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*) is "signless" (*animitta*) because of its lack of clarity.
For one who has attained that state, the perception (*saṃjñā*) does not take the object as a sign; thus, it is "having a signless object.
Because the signs (*nimitta*) are indistinct in the Peak of Existence, its object is called "signless" according to the principle of the *anudāraka* [the subtle or non-prominent].
Furthermore, it is "signless" (*animitta*) because no sign (*nimitta*) exists there at all;
otherwise, it would follow that perception itself does not exist,
since in the absence of a sign, there can be no grasping of a sign.
The desire realm is limited because it is inferior;
the form realm is "gone to greatness" (mahadgata).
Because they are supreme;
because the two immeasurables— the sphere of infinite space and the sphere of infinite consciousness— are boundless.
Because of the absence of grasping and possessions, the sphere of nothingness is "nothingness" (ākiñcanya).
Therefore, the perception that takes the desire realm and so forth as its object is called the "limited perception" and so forth.

Following the exposition of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), the exposition of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is logical, as it was listed immediately after it; therefore, the question is asked: "What are the formations?
Their exposition consists of those mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) other than feeling and perception, as well as the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*).
Because they are produced by conditions coming together and combining, all phenomena (*dharma*) comprised within the aggregates of form and so forth are called "formations."
In this context, however, only those formations (saṃskāra) comprised within the aggregate of formations (saṃskāraskandha) are intended.

This is because those comprised within the aggregates of form (rūpa), feeling (vedanā), and perception (sañjñā) have already been discussed, and those comprised within the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) will be discussed later.

For this very reason, although feeling and perception are not distinct from other mental factors (caitasika) such as contact (sparśa) and attention (manaskāra) in their nature as mental concomitants, it is said: "mental factors other than feeling and perception."

This is for the purpose of demonstrating that although feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are mental factors (*caitasika*), they are not included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*), because they are already subsumed under the aggregates of feeling and perception respectively.
For feeling is the object of experience;
indeed, it is by means of feeling that one experiences the ripening of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karmas.
Perception (*saṃjñā*) is the basis for conventional expression (*vyavahāra*).

For, by means of perception, having grasped the signs (*nimitta*) among objects seen, heard, thought, or cognized, people engage in worldly convention, saying, "It was seen," "It was heard," "It was thought," or "It was cognized. It is for this reason that feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are established as separate aggregates (*skandha*).
"Not others" refers to the mental factors (*caitasika*). If,

apart from feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*), the other mental factors beginning with contact (*sparśa*) and ending with investigation (*vicāra*), as well as the factors dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta*) such as acquisition (*prāpti*) and so forth— which are included within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*)— were [to be considered part of the aggregate of formations], then there would be a contradiction with the Sūtra.
For it is said in the Sūtra: "What is the aggregate of formations?
It is the six groups of volition.
Thus, there is no contradiction.
Because that [volition] is designated as the primary factor:

for volition (*cetanā*) is primary in the formation of the mind (*cittābhisaṃskaraṇa*), while attention (*manaskāra*) and the other factors follow it; thus, volition alone is described as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*).
For it is thus: the mind impels [itself] toward the wholesome, and it also impels [itself] toward the unwholesome and the indeterminate, as well as toward states such as pleasure and pain.
Just like the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), the mental factors (*caitasika*) are also not understood; this is the question.
"Those dharmas which are associated with the mind"—this is the answer.
Since these [factors] are not yet understood, he asks:
"The exposition is contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), and so forth.

These factors, beginning with contact and ending with investigation (vicāra), are called "associated" (samprayukta) because they are applied equally by way of the five modes of equality—equality of basis, object, aspect, time, and substance—and thus follow the mind.

Since the statement "associated with the mind" is made without qualification, it would follow that all [mental factors] are associated with every state of mind; therefore, in order to determine them, he says: "Of these, five are universal, five have specific objects, and eleven are wholesome."
The six [root] afflictions,
the remaining secondary afflictions, and the four beginning with remorse may also be otherwise.
Among these, those which are primary—contact, attention, feeling, perception, and volition—are the omnipresent factors (*sarvatraga*).
For these five dharmas follow after every state of mind; thus, they are called "omnipresent."
For these [mental factors] are associated with wholesome states of the three realms and with the untainted (anāsrava);
they are also associated with unwholesome states belonging to the desire realm, and with afflicted and neutral states belonging to the three realms.
Indeed, in all occurrences of consciousness, there must necessarily be a convergence of the triad [of faculty, object, and consciousness].
Furthermore, because the coming together of the triad is invariably accompanied by contact (*sparśa*), contact is omnipresent (*sarvatraga*).

Since there is no occurrence of a mind that is effortless (*nirābhoga*) with respect to an object, attention (*manaskāra*) is also omnipresent. And since there is no mind that is devoid of experience (*niranubhava*) or independent of the grasping of signs (*nimitta*), feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) are likewise omnipresent.
Since volition is indeed mental action, it too must necessarily be present in every state of mind; therefore, these five factors are universal.

The five with determined objects (*pratiniyataviṣaya*) are so called because their objects are restricted and not universal; they are, moreover, desire (*chanda*), resolve (*adhimokṣa*), mindfulness (*smṛti*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). Eleven [mental factors] are wholesome (*kuśala*).

Furthermore, these [factors] beginning with faith and ending with non-harming are wholesome because they are the opposites of lack of faith and so forth, and because they are associated with the roots of wholesomeness;
moreover, the mind associated with these very factors is wholesome.
There are six primary afflictions (*kleśa*): attachment, aversion, pride, ignorance, views, and doubt.
For these afflict the mind, they are thus called *kleśas*.
The remaining ones are the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*).

Furthermore, those beginning with anger (*krodha*) and ending with lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*), as well as the four beginning with remorse (*kaukṛtya*), are stated to be "otherwise"; thus, although it is mentioned without distinction that the remaining ones are secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), it is understood that they end specifically with *asamprajanya*.

They are called secondary afflictions because they are members of the primary afflictions (*kleśa*) and because they cause the defilement of the mind, thereby existing in proximity to the primary afflictions.
"The four beginning with remorse" refers to remorse (*kaukṛtya*), torpor (*middha*), applied thought (*vitarka*), and sustained thought (*vicāra*).
"Also otherwise" means that these are not only secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*); rather, they can also be wholesome (*kuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
This aggregate of mental factors, in brief, consists of fifty-one.
However, since the individual nature of each of these is not understood, the question arises: "What is contact?
What is mental attention? and so forth.
Here, the mental factors (*caitasika*) are explained by way of their characteristics alone, and not by way of their functions as is done elsewhere.

Because brevity was intended [in the previous section], we shall, however, also explain their functions for the sake of easy understanding. In that regard, their essential nature alone was previously explained.
Because it was previously mentioned;
likewise, this should be stated elsewhere as well according to the possibility.
"The determination of the conjunction of the triad" is the subject at hand; the triad consists of precisely these three: the sense faculty, the object, and consciousness.
The coexistence of these [three] through the relationship of cause and effect is *samavāya* (inherence).

When that exists, at that very moment, there occurs a modification of the sense faculty conducive to the arising of feelings such as pleasure; the discernment of the object’s aspect as being experienced as pleasure and so forth, which corresponds to that [modification], is *sparśa* (contact).

Furthermore, the faculty (*indriya*) is that by means of which a specific quality attains the state of being a cause for pleasure, pain, and so forth; the modification of that is the "modification of the faculty" (*indriya-vikāra*).
It is called "contact" (*sparśa*) because it touches the faculty through similarity, or is touched by the faculty.
Its function is to serve as the basis for feeling (*vedanā*).
For it is said thus in the Sūtra: "Dependent upon a contact to be experienced as pleasant, a pleasant feeling arises."
What is attention (*manaskāra*)?
It is the mental application (*ābhoga*) of the mind; "application" (*ābhoga*) means the act of bending toward [the object].
That by which the mind is directed toward an object is the mental application (*ābhoga*) of the mind;
furthermore, its function is to hold the mind upon the object.
Furthermore, the fixing of the mind (*cittadhāraṇa*) is the repeated directing of the mind toward that very same object.

And this function is described with reference to a specific mental attention (*manaskāra*) characterized by the restriction of the mental continuum to a single object, and not with reference to every single moment of consciousness.
As for the illustration given here— that one who has attained meditative concentration (samādhi) is said to have attained mental attention (manaskāra)—
in that case, he is called "one who has attained mental attention" precisely because of attaining a distinguished kind of mental attention;
otherwise, all sentient beings would indeed be possessors of mental attention.
Because for all [beings], there is the presence of mental attention at every moment of consciousness.
What is volition? It is the mental formation of the mind—mental action—with respect to qualities, defects, or neither. With respect to qualities means with respect to wholesome phenomena.

From the perspective of faults, [this applies] to unwholesome states; from the perspective of neither, to neutral states; or alternatively, from the perspective of qualities, to those that are beneficial.
"From the perspective of faults" refers to those who cause harm; "from neither" refers to those who are neutral. "Mental formation" (*cittābhisaṃskāra*) means the activity of the mind.
When this [mental faculty] exists, there occurs a vibration of the mind toward an object, like the vibration of iron under the influence of a magnet.
And it is said: "By which the mind does not remain for even another moment and is devoid of activity..."
That volition, which is mental action, makes it appear as if it were possessed of activity.
Thus [it is asked]: when "mental formation" (*cittābhisaṃskāra*) is stated, for what purpose is it specified as "mental action" (*manaskarma*)?
For the mind is formed by all mental factors (*caitasika*) alike.
He says "mental action" (*manaskarma*) in order to distinguish it from those [other types of action],
for the purpose of making known that the very property which is the movement of consciousness is itself volition (*cetanā*), and nothing else.
The formulation of action is "the mental formation with respect to the virtuous, the non-virtuous, or that which is neither";
the definition of the intrinsic nature of volition is "mental action."
What is desire (*chanda*)? It is the longing for an intended object.
The inclusion of the term "intended" is for the purpose of making known that there is no desire for what is not intended.
In this way, it is made known that desire (*chanda*) has a specific object.
That thing which is intended as the object of activities such as seeing and hearing is what is "intended" (*abhipreta*).
In that regard, the longing for seeing and hearing is "aspiration" (*prārthanā*).
If *chanda* consists of aspiration, what is the specific distinction between *tṛṣṇā* and *chanda*?
*Tṛṣṇā* is characterized by attachment (*abhiṣvaṅga*).
Zeal is characterized by aspiration; this is its distinction. Its function is to provide a basis for the initiation of vigor.
What is resolve (*adhimokṣa*)?
It is the ascertainment of a determined object exactly as it is; the inclusion of the term "determined" is for the purpose of indicating that resolve has all things as its object.
For it is not possible to have a definitive determination regarding an object that has not been ascertained.
An object is "ascertained" when it is free from doubt through either reasoning or the instruction of a reliable authority.
In whatever aspect it is ascertained—such as the aspects of impermanence, suffering, and so forth—[it is said to be ascertained].
Resolute conviction (*adhimokṣa*) is the fixing of that very object in the mind in its specific form, the determination that "it is exactly thus and not otherwise.
Its function is to be unshakeable;
for one whose resolute conviction is predominant cannot be led away from their own established tenet by the proponents of other doctrines.

What is mindfulness (*smṛti*)? It is the non-forgetfulness regarding a familiar object and the mental noting (*abhilapanatā*) [of it]. The term "familiar" is used for the purpose of showing that there is no mindfulness regarding what is unfamiliar.
A familiar object is one previously experienced.
Non-forgetfulness is the cause for not losing the grasping of the focal object.
It is the repeated recollection of the focal object and its aspects regarding an object previously grasped; it is the state of verbalization.
"Abhilapanam" (expressing) is like the act of expressing; "abhilapanatā" (the state of expressing) is simply the act of expressing itself.
Furthermore, when there is the expression of the object, there is no distraction of the mind toward another object or another aspect; therefore, its function is non-distraction.
What is concentration?
It is the one-pointedness of the mind upon an object to be examined;
"to be examined" means nowhere else.

And thus, it is stated that concentration has a specific object; namely, one-pointedness of mind— that is, having a single focal point— with respect to the thing under investigation, whether in terms of its qualities or its defects.
For here, the focal object (ālambana) is said to be the foremost;
its function is to provide a basis for knowledge,
because when the mind is concentrated, there is thorough knowledge of things as they truly are (yathābhūta).
The object to be examined is the fourfold truth. By way of its qualities, the truth of cessation and the truth of the path are to be examined;
the truth of cessation is to be examined through aspects such as peace and so forth.
The truth of the path is [contemplated] through aspects such as leading to liberation;
the truths of suffering and its origin are [contemplated] by way of their defects;
and suffering is [contemplated] through aspects such as impermanence.
Origination is [contemplated] through aspects such as cause and so forth;
likewise, among the nine stages, one views the lower stage as faulty and the higher stage as possessing qualities.
In this same way, it should be stated for other general objects of focus as well, according to what is applicable.
What is wisdom (*prajñā*)?
It is discernment (*pravicaya*) with respect to that very same object, whether it is produced through proper application (*yoga*), improper application (*ayoga*), or otherwise.
"With respect to that very same [object]" means with respect to the very object under investigation.
And thus it is stated that wisdom, like concentration, has a specific object.
It is called *pravicaya* because it discerns (*pravicinoti*).
It is the distinct comprehension of phenomena, whether correct or incorrect, as if their specific and general characteristics were intermingled.
Reasoning (*yukti*) is *yoga*—namely, authoritative instruction, inference, and direct perception.
That which is produced by these three modes is "prescribed by yoga" (*yogavihita*).
Furthermore, it consists of that which consists of hearing (*śrutamaya*), that which consists of reflection (*cintāmaya*), and that which consists of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).
Among these, the understanding born from the authority of the words of a reliable person is that consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya*);
that born from the contemplation of reasoning is that consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*);
and that born from meditative concentration is that consisting of cultivation (*bhāvanāmaya*).

Furthermore, non-application (*ayoga*) consists of instruction from an unreliable source, fallacious inference, and a wrongly directed meditative concentration (*samādhi*). That which is produced by these is "produced by non-application" (*ayogavihita*).
