In this regard, the wisdom consisting of hearing (*śrutamaya*) and the wisdom consisting of reflection (*cintāmaya*) belonging to the Sāṅkhyas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others, are produced by non-application because they arise from the instruction of unreliable persons and are produced by fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*).

However, for those who are free from passion but hold views of eternalism or nihilism, as well as those who maintain partial eternalism and so forth, [wisdom] is produced through improper application because it arises from a wrongly directed concentration (*mithyāpraṇihitasamādhi*).
That which is acquired at birth and the understanding of worldly conventions are neither produced through proper application nor produced through improper application.
And this [latter kind of wisdom] has the function of dispelling doubt.
The removal of doubt, however, results from the attainment of certainty by one who discriminates phenomena through wisdom.
[40] What is faith (*śraddhā*)?
It is conviction regarding action, its fruit, the truths, and the jewels; it is aspiration and clarity of mind.
Action is threefold.
It is meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable.
Among these, the non-meritorious belongs exclusively to the realm of desire,
because it is associated with the unwholesome roots.
Merit (*puṇya*) as well, by virtue of its fixed maturation (*vipākaniyama*), belongs exclusively to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
It is called "immovable" (*āniñjya*) because it does not waver with respect to the maturation of karma.
For non-merit (*apuṇya*), there is an undesirable maturation within the desire realm.
The maturation of meritorious karma is desired;
the maturation of imperturbable karma is indeed desired in the realms of form and formlessness.
In that regard, faith is the mode of conviction that both the action and its fruit exist.
There is wholesome and unwholesome karma, and that [karma] has desirable and undesirable fruits respectively;
that too has wholesome and unwholesome karma as its cause.

The firm conviction that [the world] is not created by a Lord or other such causes— this very conviction regarding the nature of action and its fruit, as well as the non-erroneous relationship between cause and fruit in the ripening of action and its fruit— is faith in the form of conviction in the existence of action and its fruit.
The truths are suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path.

The five aggregates of clinging, as the result [of suffering], constitute the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), because they are disagreeable to the noble ones and because they are non-erroneous by virtue of their impermanence and other such characteristics.

Those same five aggregates of clinging, as the cause [of suffering], constitute the truth of origin (*samudayasatya*), because they are the cause of suffering and because they are non-perverted through aspects such as conditions (*pratyaya*).

The cessation of suffering, which consists in the pacification of suffering together with its causes, constitutes the truth of cessation (*nirodhasatya*), because it is the nature of the pacification of suffering with its causes and because it is non-perverted through aspects such as peace (*śānta*).
The Noble Eightfold Path is the truth of the path because it brings about the cessation of suffering and because it is non-erroneous by virtue of its leading to liberation and so forth.
In that regard, faith toward the truths of suffering and its origin consists of the mental aspect of firm conviction that "suffering exists" and "the origin exists.
Toward the truths of cessation and the path, faith consists of the mental aspect of aspiration.
"I am able to attain cessation and to generate the path."
The Three Jewels are the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.

They are called "jewels" because they are like jewels: due to their rarity, their great value, their capacity to produce joy, their capacity to provide benefit, and their nature as an antidote to harm from non-human beings and other such threats.

Among these, their rarity is such that they are attained only after three incalculable eons by Bodhisattvas who, being unattached to the enjoyments of existence and indifferent to body and life, engage continuously in the accumulations for enlightenment.
That Buddhahood is attained is difficult to find;
for this very reason, the arising of a Buddha is said to be as rare as the appearance of the udumbara flower.
And because the arising of a Buddha is so rare, the Jewels of the Dharma and the Saṅgha are also rare, since they are dependent upon the arising of a Buddha.
Furthermore, its great value arises from the fact that it is attainable through the accumulations of merit, wisdom, and both together, which have reached the state of ultimate excellence.
In this context, the accumulation of merit consists of the three perfections of generosity, ethical discipline, and patience;
the accumulation of wisdom consists of the perfections of insight and meditative concentration.
Because it serves as the constituent factor for the accumulations of merit and wisdom, the perfection of vigor is both accumulations.
Furthermore, the Jewel of the Dharma is of great value because it is obtained through the relinquishing of all conditioned things;
likewise, the Jewel of the Saṅgha is of great value because it is obtained through the distinguished merit and wisdom that bring about results beyond the cycle of existence.
Indeed, the Three Jewels are the cause of joy because they produce joy through seeing, hearing, and recollecting them;
likewise, they bring benefit to sentient beings through approaching, attending upon, seeking, and fully understanding them.
As it is said: "Approaching you brings glory; attending upon you brings auspiciousness."
Investigation brings about intelligence; thorough knowledge leads to purification.
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, regarding the pacification of harm from non-human beings and the like, it is stated in detail in the Sūtra: "O monks, if those who have gone to the forest... [and so on] ...whatever fear, trepidation, or horripilation may arise, that shall pass away."
The same should be said regarding the recollection of the Jewel of the Dharma and the recollection of the Jewel of the Saṅgha.

In that regard, the Buddha is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) resulting from the attainment of the power of knowledge that is unattached and unimpeded with respect to all that is knowable.
Furthermore, that [transformation] is devoid of all seeds of contaminated phenomena (*sāsravadharma*) and is accumulated with all seeds of uncontaminated phenomena (*anāsravadharma*).
Possessing infinite power, it is like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇiratna), capable of accomplishing the welfare of all sentient beings without effort.
Dharmas are threefold:
the dharma of teaching, consisting of the sūtras, geyas, and so forth;
and the dharma of practice, consisting of the noble eightfold path along with its ancillaries.
The ultimate reality (*paramārthadharma*) is *nirvāṇa*. It is of two kinds: with a remainder of substrate (*sopadhiśeṣa*) and without a remainder of substrate (*nirupadhiśeṣa*).
Among these, that which is called the dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśavisaṃyoga*) is "with a remainder of substrate."
Upon the cessation of the present birth, the non-arising of future births is the nirvāṇa without remainder (nirupadhiśeṣa).
The Saṅgha consists of eight types of persons: the four who have entered the paths and the four who abide in the fruits.
It is called the Saṅgha because it cannot be divided from one another nor from the Teacher.

Faith, characterized by clarity and indicated by such signs as horripilation and the shedding of tears, is directed toward the Blessed Buddha, because he has reached the ultimate limit of the excellence of all virtues and the removal of all faults.

Faith is characterized by clarity regarding the Dharma because it consists in the pacification of all suffering along with its causes, because it brings about that pacification, and because it illuminates it.
It likewise consists in clarity regarding the Saṅgha because they have crossed over the mire of saṃsāra and because they stand upon the path for crossing over the mire of saṃsāra.
For faith indeed operates in three ways:
it has the aspect of conviction toward an existing thing, whether it possesses qualities or lacks them;
and it has the aspect of serene confidence toward an existing thing that possesses qualities.
And when a virtuous quality is present, attainable, and capable of being produced, it takes the form of longing (*abhilāṣa*).
[Objection: But if it is thus of the nature of longing, does it not become either craving (*tṛṣṇā*) or desire (*chanda*)?
[Response: This is not so.
Because it has wholesome objects, it is not craving;
because desire is preceded by faith, it is not desire;
it is the clarity of the mind.

Since faith (*śraddhā*) is indeed the opposite of mental turbidity, when it is associated with it, the mind becomes clear through the removal of the turbidity of the stains of the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*). Thus, by relying on faith, the mind becomes serene; this is called "serenity of the mind" (*cetasaḥ prasādaḥ*). To demonstrate that faith is a distinct mental factor (*caitasika*) comparable to a water-clearing gem, and not of the nature of physical clarity (*rūpaprasāda*), he says: "serenity of the mind."
It is clarity of mind,
not of form;
furthermore, its function is to provide a basis for desire.
What is *hrī*? It is shame regarding a fault, taking oneself or the Dharma as the dominant influence (*adhipati*).
That which is dependent upon which [influence], such that one's engagement in or withdrawal from actions occurs, that is its dominant influence; the meaning is "its master" (*svāmī*).
Taking oneself, the Dharma, or the sovereign master as the authority,
that which is blameworthy (*avadya*) is precisely evil (*pāpa*), because it is censured by the virtuous and because its maturation is undesirable.
The shrinking of the mind (*avalīnatā*) due to such a blameworthy act— whether committed or uncommitted— is shame (*lajjā*).
Having considered oneself unfit for sinful action due to qualities such as noble birth, knowledge, and so forth— thinking,

"How indeed could such a person as I have committed, is committing, or will commit such a sin? Even in the case of [so-called] dharma, this is censurable because its ripening is undesirable and because it involves the infliction of harm upon others"— the shame felt by one who thus reflects upon oneself and dharma regarding that fault is [the sense of shame].
That is moral shame (*hrī*).
And its function is to provide a basis for the restraint of misconduct.
What is shame (*apatrāpya*)?
It is the feeling of shame regarding a fault, having made the world one's authority;
for this is censured in the world.
One feels shame regarding a fault out of fear of ill-repute and the like, thinking, "Knowing me to be one who acts in this way, they will censure me.
This too has the function of providing a basis for the restraint of misconduct;
restraint is the desisting from misconduct.

Because one who feels shame (*lajjamāna*) or experiences moral dread (*apatrapamāṇa*) necessarily desists from even committed misconduct, these two have the function of providing a basis for that desistance.
Regarding the term *alobha*: this negative particle (*a-*) functions in three senses: [it denotes] non-existence, ...
And regarding "another antidote":
he says "the antidote to greed" in order to demonstrate that it exists here as an antidote itself, and not as something else, nor as a mere absence.
The same should be stated for non-hatred and non-delusion.

Disenchantment (*nirvid*) and non-clinging (*anāgraha*): this is the definition of their essential nature. What is called greed (*lobha*) is attachment to and longing for existence and the requisites of existence.
Its opposite, non-greed (*alobha*), is non-attachment to and aversion toward existence and the requisites of existence.
Disgust (*nirvid*) is the turning away from existence and the enjoyments of existence due to a thorough understanding of their defects.
Non-attachment (*anāgraha*) is the lack of clinging to existence and the enjoyments of existence.

Alternatively, the term "disgust" is included for the purpose of qualifying non-attachment: that non-attachment which takes the form of turning away from existence and the enjoyments of existence is what is meant by "non-greed" (*alobha*).
And this has the function of providing a basis for the non-occurrence of misconduct.
What is non-hatred?
It is loving-kindness (*maitrī*), which is the antidote to hatred.
For hatred is malice toward sentient beings, toward suffering, and toward those things that are the basis for suffering.
Its antidote is non-malice (*anāghāta*).
Since there are other antidotes to hatred as well, he says: "loving-kindness" (*maitrī*).
That which is the antidote to hatred, consisting of loving-kindness, is non-hatred (*adveṣa*).
"Not another" means that this [non-violence] also has the function of providing a basis for the non-engagement in misconduct.
What is non-delusion? It is the antidote to delusion; it is correct realization of reality.

For all wholesome factors are indeed antidotes to afflicted factors because they are incompatible with the manifestation of those afflicted factors; therefore, it is said: "correct realization of reality."
This is due to the distinction between correct and non-perverted practice.
Furthermore, it is of two kinds: knowledge (*jñāna*) and analytical reflection (*pratisaṅkhyā*).
Moreover, it is of four kinds, having as its causes maturation (*vipāka*), scripture (*āgama*), reflection (*cintā*), and realization (*adhigama*).
Discernment (*pratisaṅkhyā*), however, is wisdom (*prajñā*) itself accompanied by steadfastness (*dhairya*).
By "steadfastness," wisdom, vigor (*vīrya*), and concentration (*samādhi*) are meant.
Since it is impossible for two instances of the substance of wisdom to coexist, wisdom that is associated with either vigor or concentration is called discernment.
By the power of which, even though the seeds of the afflictions have not been uprooted or destroyed, one does not grant them any opportunity;

this is the meaning of the statement here: non-delusion (*amoha*) is said to be a specific kind of knowledge consisting of the cognition of things as they truly are (*yathābhūtajñāna*) and characterized by analytical discernment (*pratisaṃkhyā*). For this very reason, non-delusion has the function of providing a basis for the non-occurrence of misconduct.
What is vigor (*vīrya*)?
It is the antidote to laziness (*kausīdya*), the mental enthusiasm for what is wholesome.
One is called "lazy" (*kusīda*) because one sinks (*sīdati*) into what is contemptible (*kutsita*).
Its state is laziness;
the meaning is indolence.
And that is the lack of enthusiasm of the mind toward what is wholesome and unwholesome.

And since vigor (*vīrya*) is the antidote to that [laziness], he says—following the same logic as for laziness when both possibilities arise—in order to exclude [the unwanted case]: "Vigor is the mental exertion toward the wholesome, but not toward the afflicted. For exertion toward the afflicted is indeed laziness, because it is contemptible.
But surely, because it is thoroughly habituated, the afflicted mind proceeds by its own natural force; what need is there for exertion in that regard?
Generally speaking, this is indeed so.
However, there is something where even enthusiasm (*utsāha*) is required;

that is to say, through its association with it, there is an exertion of the mind toward wholesome qualities (*kuśaladharma*)— whether in donning the armor, in application, in non-laxity, in non-retrogression, or in non-contentment— that is vigor (*vīrya*).
Its function is the fulfillment and perfection of the side of wholesome qualities.
Fulfillment is, for example, the initial entry into the fundamental state;
perfection is the state of having completed the preparatory cultivation of that very same state.
What is pliancy (*prasrabdhi*)?
It is the antidote to rigidity (*dauṣṭhulya*), consisting in the serviceability (*karmaṇyatā*) of body and mind.
Rigidity is the unserviceability of body and mind, as well as the seeds of defiled phenomena (*sāṅkleṣika-dharma*).
Upon the removal of that [rigidity], because pliancy (*prasrabdhi*) exists, it is the antidote to *dauṣṭhulya*.

As for the characteristic of pliancy, it is the serviceability (*karmaṇyatā*) of body and mind. Among these, the serviceability of the body is that from which the body’s lightness in its own activities arises.

Mental pliancy (*cittakarmaṇyatā*) is a distinct mental factor that serves as the cause of joy and lightness for one engaged in correct attention (*samyag-manasikāra*). Because of its association with this, the mind proceeds toward its object without attachment; therefore, it is called "mental pliancy. Furthermore, bodily pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) should be understood as a specific kind of tangible object brought forth by joy.

Because of the statement in the Sūtra, "The body of one whose mind is joyful becomes pliant," and because this context concerns mental factors (*caitasika*), even non-mental bodily pliancy (*kāyaprasrabdhi*) is described as the factor of enlightenment known as pliancy (*prasrabdhi-saṃbodhyaṅga*);
or, since bodily serviceability (*kāyakarmaṇyatā*) brings about mental serviceability (*cittakarmaṇyatā*), even non-mental bodily serviceability is mentioned here.
And by the power of this [wisdom], through the revolution of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), its function is the extraction of all obscurations, such as those of the afflictions.

What is heedfulness (*apramāda*)? It is the antidote to heedlessness (*pramāda*), consisting of non-attachment (*alobha*) up to vigor (*vīrya*); relying upon these, one abandons unwholesome states (*akuśala-dharma*).
And one cultivates the wholesome factors that are their antidotes.

For negligence is that by which one does not protect the mind from the afflictions and causes the abandonment of the wholesome; whereas through non-negligence, one abandons the afflictions and cultivates the factors that are their antidotes. Therefore, non-negligence is said to be the antidote to negligence.
"From non-attachment up to vigor"—by this, non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion are taken together with vigor.

By the statement, "relying upon, resorting to, and attaining these qualities beginning with non-attachment and ending with vigor, one abandons unwholesome states," it is thereby said that all [these] factors from non-attachment onwards constitute heedfulness (*apramāda*).
Unwholesome states should be understood as the outflows (*āsrava*) and the objects conducive to the outflows.
In this context, abandonment consists of the dispelling, the suppression, and the uprooting of the seeds of the outflows (*āsrava*).
Furthermore, there is abandonment through the complete avoidance of sense objects.
"Their antidotes" refers to the antidotes to unwholesome factors (*akuśaladharma*).
Furthermore, those [factors] are both wholesome-with-outflows and without-outflows;
their cultivation (*bhāvanā*) is their repeated bringing into manifestation.

Because one abandons unwholesome states and cultivates their antidotes by relying on non-attachment and the other [wholesome roots] accompanied by vigor, heedfulness (apramāda) is designated in relation to non-attachment and the rest when they are conjoined with vigor. By this, the designation of heedfulness is stated as having both a basis and a cause.
Furthermore, its function is the fulfillment of all mundane and supramundane perfections.
In this context, mundane prosperity is the attainment of excellence regarding existence and enjoyments; supramundane prosperity is the realization of the enlightenment of the Śrāvakas and so forth.
What is equanimity (*upekṣā*)?
It is that same non-attachment (*alobha*), up to and including vigor (*vīrya*), and so forth—the explanation here is similar to that of heedfulness (*apramāda*).
By means of the three terms beginning with "evenness of mind" (*cittasamatā*), the initial, middle, and final stages of equanimity are illuminated.
In this context, laxity (*laya*) and excitement (*auddhatya*) constitute an unevenness of the mind.
Due to their absence, there is initially an evenness (*samatā*) of the mind.
Thereafter, for the concentrated mind that proceeds without deliberate effort or exertion, its functioning in accordance with its natural state as it truly is constitutes "smoothness" (*praśaṭhatā*).
Furthermore, that state is accompanied by the apprehension of lethargy and excitement because it has not yet been cultivated for long.

Then, through reaching the culmination of cultivation and the distancing of those opposing factors, when that apprehension ceases, the mind enters a state of effortlessness (*anābhoga*)— a state of non-exertion for one who no longer applies directed attention (*ābhoga*) toward the objects that serve as antidotes to lethargy and excitement.

"In which afflicted phenomena have been expelled"— here, "by which" refers specifically to equanimity (*upekṣā*). Afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭa-dharma*) are those accompanied by passion (*rāga*) and so forth.
Their "expulsion" (*nirvāsana*) means non-arising again.

Since equanimity (*upekṣā*) is indeed the opposite of dwelling in affliction (*saṅkliṣṭa-vihāra*), it must necessarily function as an obstacle to the activity of passion and so forth; therefore, it is said that they have been "expelled by it. And because equanimity is incompatible with dwelling in affliction, [the text speaks of their expulsion].
Thus, by dwelling in equanimity, one becomes a dweller free from affliction;
therefore, equanimity has the function of providing a basis that allows no opportunity for affliction.
What is non-violence?
It is compassion, which is the antidote to violence.
Non-violence is the absence of harm and the absence of malice toward sentient beings through killing, binding, and so forth; it is the antidote to violence.
"Karunā" means that which obstructs "ka"; "ka" is a designation for happiness;
thus, the meaning is that it obstructs happiness.
For one who is compassionate indeed suffers with the suffering of others; and this [compassion], like heedfulness (*apramāda*), exists only as a designation (*prajñapti*),
not as a substantial entity (*dravyasat*).
Because it is designated as a portion of non-hatred,
its function is non-violence.
Thus, the eleven wholesome [factors] have been explained.
The six afflictions are to be explained; they are stated as follows: What is attachment (*rāga*)?
It is affection for and clinging to the five aggregates of grasping (*pañca-upādānaskandha*).
The five contaminated aggregates of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are the aggregates of clinging to form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Among these, the aggregate of clinging to form consists of the form belonging to the two realms;
the four aggregates of clinging to feeling and so forth consist of the feelings and so on belonging to the three realms.
By means of this craving (*tṛṣṇā*), the arising of the three realms of existence or karma leading to rebirth is grasped; thus, craving is called "grasping" (*upādāna*).
Because they are produced from grasping, because they are subject to grasping, or because they arise from those [other factors], they are the "aggregates of grasping" (*upādānaskandha*).
It is like "affection" (*sneha*) in the sense of being sticky or adhesive.

For just as an oily substance such as oil, having entered its substrate such as cloth, pervades it and is difficult to separate from its substrate even with great effort, so too passion, having entered its very object, pervades it and is difficult to separate from that object even with great exertion; thus it is called "oiliness" (sneha).
Adhyavasāna is absorption in that [object].
Alternatively, in order to distinguish it from "moisture" (sneha), which is also a specific kind of tangible object, he says: "adhyavasāna.
Furthermore, its function is the production of suffering.

Because they are associated with the three types of suffering, the five aggregates of the three realms are intended as "suffering" according to their respective occurrence; and since that suffering is produced through the power of craving for the desire, form, and formless realms, the function of attachment is specified as the generation of suffering.
What is hostility (*pratigha*)? It is malice (*āghāta*) toward sentient beings.
Malice is a harsh state of mind toward sentient beings, possessed of which one contemplates harm such as killing or binding them.
Furthermore, its function is to provide a basis for an unpleasant state of existence and for misconduct.
"Sparśa" means happiness; an abiding accompanied by that is "sparśavihāra."
"Not dwelling in comfort" means not dwelling in a state free from contact; the meaning is that it is accompanied by suffering.
Because mental distress (*daurmanasya*) necessarily arises for one whose mind is full of malice (*āghāta*), the mind is tormented.
And because the body conforms to the mind, it too is indeed tormented;

thus, in all postures, his dwelling becomes one accompanied by suffering and distress. Furthermore, for one whose mind is obstructed, no misconduct is far off—thus, aversion (*pratigha*) is said to have the function of providing a basis for dwelling in discomfort and for misconduct.
What is pride?
It consists of the seven types of pride; for all pride indeed proceeds by relying upon the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
It has the characteristic of uplifting the mind.

For, having superimposed the state of "self" and "mine" upon the aggregates, one thinks "I am this" and "this is mine," and by various such distinctions, one uplifts oneself and considers oneself superior to others.
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of disrespect and suffering.
Lack of respect toward gurus and toward individuals endowed with virtuous qualities, as well as arrogance and the withdrawal of body and speech [from them], leads to the arising of suffering;
here, the "arising of suffering" should be understood as the arising of renewed existence (*punarbhava*).

Furthermore, although there is no difference in its essential nature as an inflation of the mind (*cittonnati*), it is divided into seven types based on the differences in the causes for that inflation—namely, pride (*māna*), excessive pride (*atimāna*), and so forth.
The inflation of the mind thinking "I am superior" in terms of family, knowledge, wealth, and so forth, compared to one who is inferior in family, knowledge, wealth, and so forth;
or the inflation of the mind thinking "I am equal" in terms of those very same factors such as family when compared with an equal—
that is pride (*māna*).

Excessive pride (*atimāna*) is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I am superior" to one who is equal in terms of family, knowledge, wealth, and so forth, due to [one's own] generosity, ethical conduct, prowess, and so forth; or, "I am equal" to one who is superior in terms of family, wealth, and so forth, due to [one's own] knowledge, wealth, and so forth.
This is excessive pride.

Pride beyond pride (*mānātimāna*) is that inflation of the mind which thinks, "I alone am superior in terms of lineage, knowledge, and wealth" regarding one who is actually superior in lineage, knowledge, and wealth; this is pride beyond pride. Pride of "I am" (*asmimāna*) refers to [the inflation of the mind] regarding the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*).
For here, desire and lust constitute grasping (*upādāna*).
Desire is the longing for a future self-existence;
lust is the attachment to the present.
Therein, one takes up a future personal existence by way of desire;
one takes up the present aggregates by way of passion, through not relinquishing them.
Therefore, these two alone are called "clinging" (*upādāna*).
The aggregates associated with that [clinging] are the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*).

The inflation of the mind (*cittasyonnati*) resulting from the adherence to a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīyābhiniveśa*) toward those aggregates of clinging— which are devoid of a self and what belongs to a self—
is this "I-am" conceit (*asmimāna*).
Conceit (*abhimāna*) is the inflation of the mind consisting in the thought "I have attained" regarding a superior distinction that has not yet been attained.
Human qualities (*manuṣyadharma*) are passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth,
as well as the actions of body, speech, and mind set in motion by them.

That which serves as its antidote— namely, the meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), attainments (*samāpatti*), and so forth— is called the "superior distinction" (*uttariviśeṣa*) over human qualities. When that superior distinction has not yet been attained, the inflation of the mind thinking, "I have attained the superior distinction," is [conceit].
That is overweening pride (*abhimāna*).

Inferiority-pride (*ūnamāna*) is the inflation of the mind [thinking], "I am only slightly inferior in terms of family, learning, wealth, and so forth, compared to one who is vastly superior in family, learning, wealth, and so forth.
It is indeed appropriate that one who is equal [should think] they are equal; [but this is not the case here].
Pride (*māna*) arises from the state of being elevated, whether by thinking "I am superior to my equals" or "I am superior to those who are superior.
But for one who perceives oneself as inferior, what state of elevation could there be?

For this reason, pride is said to belong to him; this very state of loftiness consists in thinking, "I am only slightly inferior to those who are vastly superior," rather than [thinking] "I am vastly inferior.
Furthermore, there are some who, even though they are inferior to the preeminent mass of sentient beings, highly esteem themselves.
False pride (*mithyāmāna*) is that inflation of the mind whereby one who lacks virtues thinks, "I am virtuous.
Virtues (*guṇa*) are giving, ethical discipline, patience, and so forth;
he in whom these do not exist is "one who lacks virtues" (*aguṇavat*).
Alternatively, "defects" (*aguṇa*) refers to immorality and so forth. One who possesses these is "one who has defects.
Therefore, [the conceit] is: "I am one who has virtues," when one actually lacks virtues.

Regarding the phrase "one who lacks qualities": by this, it is implied that one accepts the possession of qualities despite the absence of virtues such as generosity and ethical conduct; therefore, because it is devoid of a real basis, it is called false pride (*mithyāmāna*).
What is ignorance?
It is non-knowledge regarding karma, its fruit, the truths, and the jewels.
Furthermore, it is both innate and conceptually constructed.
In that context, it is "unshared" (*āveṇikī*) because it is not associated with other secondary afflictions (*kleśa*).
It is "conceptualized" when it is associated with afflictions such as doubt, wrong view, and the adherence to rites and rituals.
Regarding karma, ignorance is that lack of knowledge, non-comprehension, and non-awakening concerning the existence of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma.
This is innate ignorance (*sahajāvidyā*): it belongs to those who,
being skeptical or disparaging regarding the existence of meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable karma, think "there is no merit, no demerit,
and no imperturbable [karma]," or to those who perceive as non-meritorious the merit found in abstaining from animal sacrifice, entering fire, and so forth.
The ignorance associated with wrong view that arises as doubt regarding what is non-meritorious— such as animal sacrifice or entering fire— yet is perceived by those who believe it to be meritorious,
is the imagined [ignorance].
Its function is to provide a basis for the arising of afflictions through false certainty and doubt regarding phenomena.

Since wisdom (*prajñā*) characterized by discernment is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*), when there is the possibility of including mundane right view (*laukikī-samyagdṛṣṭi*) and so forth, [the author], demonstrating that the five views beginning with the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) are intended here by the term "view," says:
"the five views.

Although these are indistinguishable in their afflicted nature, he speaks again—starting with "the view of a self-identity" and "the view of grasping at extremes"—in order to demonstrate their distinctions based on differences in objective referent (*ālambana*) and aspect (*ākāra*).
It is called "sat" because it exists (*sīdati*);
"kāya" means an accumulation (*caya*).
Thus, it is made known that this view applies to a perishable composite, and not to a self or anything belonging to a self.
For the proponents of a self (*ātmavādin*) maintain that the self is eternal and unitary;
thus, it is implied that this [cognition], because its objects are impermanent and manifold, does not have the self as its object.

Regarding the passage beginning with "the five aggregates of clinging" (*pañcopādānaskandhān*): whatever ascetics or brahmins perceive a self or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*), they perceive [only] these.
Regarding this, it is stated in the Sūtra: "These are simply these five aggregates of clinging.
For they might designate a self either by way of its intrinsic nature or by way of its function.
The Sāṅkhyas, for instance, consider the self to have the nature of consciousness.
And being ignorant of the distinctions between mind and mental factors, they claim that the entire aggregate of mind and mental factors is itself consciousness;
therefore, they have apprehended the four aggregates as the self,
and the aggregate of form as belonging to the self.
Furthermore, it is not possible for one with a healthy mind to describe or comprehend consciousness as something other than a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*).

Thus, regarding those such as the Vedāntins and certain Nirgranthas who maintain that the self (*ātman*) has the nature of knowledge, their grasping at a self and what belongs to a self (*ātmātmīya-grāha*) should be understood as being exactly as described immediately above.
The Vaiśeṣikas and others, however, designate the self by its effects—that which sees, and so on, up to that which thinks.
Likewise, for those who hold that "the self is that which feels, knows, remembers,
wills, and discerns," their conceit of a self is likewise directed toward the eyes and other sense faculties alone.
Because there is no seer distinct from the eye;
for the designation "seeing" applies to visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
Since the eye is its specific cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇa*), it is conventionally expressed that "the eye sees."
For example, because it is the uncommon cause of the sound, one says "the bell rings.
But in that case where, having seen forms with the eye, one is neither glad nor sad, how is it there?
In that regard as well, it is precisely where there is a designation of a self— whether in a collection or in a continuum— that it is said, "having seen forms with the eye.
For the seeing of form is nothing other than the very appearance of form.
Because the appearance and non-appearance of form are established based on the presence or absence of that [eye];
the same should be stated for hearing and so forth.
However, as for where it was said that "it feels, therefore it is sensation" (*vedanā*):
Thus, up to "it cognizes," it is called consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In this context, the designation of an agent is used merely to denote the existence [of the process], for the purpose of negating a cognizer distinct from consciousness.
The same should be stated regarding sensation and the other [aggregates].
Alternatively, the designation of "agent" is based on the appearance of the object,
as was stated previously.
Furthermore, no action exists apart from the acquisition of its own self-nature,
because all things are momentary and thus do not persist at the time of the action;
nor does there exist an action without an agent.
Furthermore, if the destruction of entities did not occur immediately after their acquisition of selfhood because it would lack a cause,
then it would not occur later either,
since there is no subsequent excellence in the nature of the destroyer or of the destruction itself.

Furthermore, in the conceptualization of destruction as having a cause, one must conceive of either that which has already perished as the cause of destruction, or something distinct from it. In the first case, it follows that the destruction of entities occurs immediately after they have acquired their own nature,
or else that there is no destruction at all.
That which is independent of others and was not previously a cause for something cannot be its cause even later,
because there is no excellence (atiśaya) in its own nature.
Even in the other case, there would be no restriction on the causes of destructions.
[Objection: Just as there is a restriction of causes for effects, there will likewise be a restriction of causes for their destructions.
[Response: This is not so.
For since effects possess mutually distinct natures, there is no contradiction in the restriction [of causes] based on the differentiation of the capacities of their respective causes.
However, since destructions are indefinable (*nirupākhyatva*) and thus lack any internal excellence (*ātmātiśaya*), by what could such a restriction be produced?
Therefore, either every cause of destruction would lead to the destruction of everything, or...
Alternatively, it should be understood that there is no cause for destruction at all;
for if destruction already exists even prior to the cause of destruction,
then it would follow that the cause of destruction is redundant.
Furthermore, if there is arising upon the destruction of entities, it would follow that even those things already destroyed could arise.

If, on the other hand, [the effect] does not exist prior to its causes of destruction, then, in that case, non-existence (abhāva) would likewise possess prior non-existence (prāgabhāva), just like an entity (bhāva).
And for that which has prior non-existence (prāgabhāva),
since it must necessarily be an entity, it must also possess posterior non-existence (pradhvaṃsābhāva).
Thus, because there would be no distinction between existence and non-existence, it would follow that everything is either of the nature of existence or of the nature of non-existence.
And if there were also a non-existence of the non-existence by destruction (pradhvaṃsābhāva), then,
because of this infinite regress of non-existences by destruction, there would likewise be an infinite regress of their causes; yet this is not accepted.

This being the case, the non-existence consisting in the destruction of an entity (*bhāva-pradhvaṃsābhāva*) should likewise not be accepted, since neither of the two lacks any specific excellence of self-nature (*ātmātiśaya*).
Furthermore, action (*kriyā*) must be conceived as either different from or non-different from entities;
if it were non-different, [the following would apply].
It is not tenable that the self alone is both the agent and the action of the self;
for if it performs an action after having already attained its own being, that action is not its essential nature.
For that which exists even without another cannot logically be considered its own nature;
and agency is not tenable in one who is devoid of action.
And since that which is superposed with activity is entirely distinct from that which is devoid of activity, how could activity be the very self of either the agent or the object?
Furthermore, because the coexistence of that which is devoid of activity and that which is superposed with it is never observed, one must admit that the former perishes and the latter arises.
Now, [if you argue that the agent] has not yet acquired its own nature...
Even so, its status as an agent and the action’s identity with it are not tenable,
because both are non-existent;
furthermore, because a single entity is devoid of action.
Because the second [moment] is superposed with activity, it lacks agency;
and due to the absence of an agent, there is also the absence of activity.
Thus, because of its destruction by its own inherent nature, momentariness itself is effectively admitted.
There is no action whatsoever other than that of the agent and the object;
for action is produced by the factors of action (kārakas),
and because it is produced, it is indeed the object (karman).

Furthermore, since neither action nor an agent is tenable without activity, there must necessarily be another action therein; and if yet another [action] were required for that, there would be an infinite regress of actions and agents.
Now, if it is argued that an action is produced without depending on another action, [the response follows].
If that is the case, why is it not accepted that the substance itself—devoid of any other action—is what is produced?
What is the use of postulating an action that is a distinct entity and whose nature and capacity are unobserved?
Moreover, if action is produced by the causal factors (kārakas), [then...]
It is not a substance;
likewise, prior non-existence and posterior non-existence belong only to action, not to substance; thus, all substances are eternal.
Or rather, one must accept that they do not exist at all;
for if the action were distinct from the factors of action, then the means of accomplishment would be devoid of action.
Thus, there would be either an infinite regress of actions or an absence of means; and due to the absence of means, there would also be an absence of action,
for there is no action that exists without a means.
And if the going were different from the goer, and the cooking different from the rice grains, then,
this being the case, the goer would not attain another location.
Or, [one might argue] that the cooking of rice grains is not a modification because they remain unchanged from their prior state;
however, if it is held that action itself is the cause of modification for its own substratum, then their being modified from their prior state remains unrefuted.
For a modification is a specific excellence (atiśaya) of the self over its prior state,
and that is invariably concomitant with difference.

Therefore, since there is necessarily no simultaneity between the preceding and succeeding states, one must admit that the arising of the subsequent state occurs at a time non-different from the destruction of the preceding one.
Thus, since action lacks a substratum and is therefore unstable, how could it be the cause of transformation?

Therefore, this grasping at "self" and "mine"—which is preceded by the grasping at a permanent agent and enjoyer—occurs only with respect to the five appropriated aggregates (*upādānaskandha*). These aggregates are devoid of activity, perish immediately after attaining their own existence, and lack an internal operative person; yet, by their mere presence, they are established as the causal basis for other aggregates that did not previously exist.
"Neither in the self nor in what belongs to the self":
by saying "as a self and as belonging to a self," he distinguishes this from the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*). "Observing" means determining.
Regarding the phrase "that which is afflicted wisdom": for one who is not deluded, the cognition that there is a self in what is not-self does not arise;
therefore, because it is associated with delusion and is erroneous, it is afflicted.
In that regard, one regards those belonging to one's own continuum as the self,
and those belonging to the continua of others— as well as those that are unappropriated— as "belonging to the self" (mine).
This is also the case when one regards even a single portion of those belonging to one's own continuum as the self.
At that time, one regards others as well as belonging to oneself;
and this [view] has the function of providing a basis for all types of views.
"Making that very [view] the dominant factor" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Because it arises through the power of the view of a self-identity,
the view of a self-identity is its dominant factor.
"Either as eternal or as annihilated"— that very thing which is apprehended as a real entity through the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is [viewed] as "eternal," meaning as permanent;
"as annihilated" means here that annihilation is a destruction without reconnection (*apratisandhika*).
One should state, as before, that this is the afflicted wisdom of one who views [them] in such a way.
Furthermore, its function is to obstruct the departure via the middle way.
The middle way is the knowledge of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) that is free from the grasping at permanence and annihilation.
[Page 62] Denying the cause, or the fruit, or the action; or destroying an existing entity, and so forth— namely, wholesome conduct and the like,
happy and miserable rebirths,
and actions such as those toward one's mother.
And the Arhat and so forth correspond respectively to the cause and so forth.
This [wrong view] has the function of severing the roots of merit and the function of providing a firm basis for the roots of non-merit;
however, it is only that which is specific [and not all such views].

What is the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*)? It is called the adherence to views because it regards views and so forth as supreme. And those very three kinds of views are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*), and false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*).
"And the aggregates which are its basis" refers to those things designated as the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of the seer,
depending upon which views arise.
They have that as their basis.
[The terms] "foremost," "best," "distinguished," and "supreme"—
these words, although having the same meaning, are employed here as successive explanations of one another.
And this [ignorance] has the function of providing a basis for adherence to false views.
Because it grasps the characteristic of a view as having the nature of a quality, it is said that this [ignorance] is the basis for all views by way of not abandoning them.
"Ethical discipline (śīla), vows (vrata), and the aggregates (skandhas) based upon them.
Here, ethical discipline is the abstention from immorality;
a vow is the restriction regarding one's dress, livelihood, and the activities of body and speech.

Those aggregates (*skandha*) depending upon which morality (*śīla*) or ascetic observance (*vrata*) proceeds are the "aggregates that are the basis for morality and ascetic observances" (*śīlavratāśraya*).

Grasping a contemptible view as being virtuous, and then regarding the morality or ascetic observance preceded by that [view] as supreme, is the "clinging to morality and ascetic observances" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).

For this very reason, the adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) was mentioned before the adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). It is "purification" (*śuddhi*) because one is purified from the accumulation of evil by means of this rule or observance;
it is "liberation" (*mukti*) because one is liberated from the bondage of the afflictions (*kleśa*) by means of this.
"Niryāṇa" means that by means of this, one goes forth from cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*).
"Nairyāṇika" means the path to liberation (*mokṣamārga*) which is itself the going forth; such is the meaning.
"Samanupaśyataḥ" means of one who examines.
The adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) is a form of wisdom characterized by the conviction that purity and so forth reside in ethical discipline or ascetic vows.
It is "afflicted" (*kliṣṭā*) because its object is erroneous.
Its function is to provide a basis for fruitless exertion.
What is doubt? It is the state of indecision regarding the truths and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," the fruits of karma and the jewels are included.
Doubt (*vimati*) is a twofold state of mind, thinking "it might be" or "it might not be. Furthermore, this should be regarded as a distinct category from wisdom (*prajñā*).
Its function is to provide a basis for the non-engagement with the side of the wholesome.

Regarding the afflictions such as attachment and so forth, how many are merely imagined (*parikalpita*) and how many are both innate (*sahaja*) and imagined? He says: "Three views are merely imagined.
Since those [three] also exist among the preceding ones, he says: "the latter [three]."
Furthermore, these are wrong view, adherence to views, and adherence to rules and rituals;
not only these are imagined,
but doubt as well is imagined.
The remaining [afflictions] are both innate (*sahaja*) and conceptually constructed (*parikalpita*).
Which, then, are the remaining ones?
They are attachment (*rāga*), hostility (*pratigha*), pride (*māna*), ignorance (*avidyā*), the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), and the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*).
The afflictions have been explained; now the secondary afflictions must be discussed. They are stated as follows:
"the present" means that which has arisen.
It is neither future nor past.
By the phrase "having encountered harm" (*apakāram āgamya*), which means "having grasped harm," he defines the object of anger;
for anger indeed proceeds only when directed toward an object that is currently undergoing harm.
"Not elsewhere" means that here too— in the phrase "malice of the mind"— both its connection with consciousness and its essential nature have been defined.
Furthermore, because its essential nature is malice (*āghāta*), it does not differ from hostility (*pratigha*).
Rather, it is a specific portion of *pratigha* (hostility),
because it is designated as a particular aspect of hostility.

Anger (*krodha*) is designated as that mental resentment directed toward a present harm, which has sentient or non-sentient beings as its object, and whose function is to provide a basis for taking up sticks and other such weapons.

Enmity (*upanāha*) is the persistence, or non-abandonment, of that hostile disposition consisting of the thought, "After my anger has subsided, this person has done me this wrong," and its continuous operation;
its function is to provide a basis for intolerance.
Intolerance (*akṣānti*) is the inability to endure harm;
it means the desire to retaliate.
This, like anger (*krodha*), is designated based on a particular state of aversion (*pradveṣa*); thus, it should be understood as being nominally existent (*prajñaptisat*).

*Mrakṣa* (concealment) is the hiding of one's faults through a portion of delusion, when one is questioned by an accuser who—having set aside desire, hatred, fear, and so forth—and seeking one’s welfare, asks at the proper time, "Did you do such a thing?
Its nature as a portion of delusion is due to its mode of concealing. Its function is to provide a basis for remorse and for dwelling in discomfort.
This is the nature of things: for one who conceals their transgression, there arises remorse;
and because of remorse, there is inevitably an association with mental distress, which results in a state of non-comfortable abiding.
Fierce speech is intense harshness by way of piercing the vital points;
one who has the habit of such [speech] is a "dāśī," and the state of being that is "dāśitā."
And this suffix denoting an abstract state (*bhāvapratyaya*) is used in its own sense (*svārthika*).
One who bites with fierce speech is "one who bites with fierce speech" (*caṇḍavacodāśitā*); this is *pradāśa*.
And since this has the nature of a mental resentment preceded by anger and enmity, it is merely a portion of hostility (*pratigha*) and does not exist as a separate substance.
And this [unwholesome action] has as its function the production of verbal misconduct and as its function the state of dwelling in discomfort,
because a person possessing it is difficult to live with.
Envy (*īrṣyā*) is a state of mental resentment belonging to the portion of hatred, which arises upon perceiving qualities such as honor, family, conduct, and learning.
"Resentment" (*vyāroṣa*) is anger that pervades one's own disposition.

Because it is associated with mental distress (*daurmanasya*), and because it is preceded by that [distress], it results in an unpleasant dwelling; thus, its function is mental distress and an unpleasant dwelling.

Giving (*dāna*) is that by which an acquired object— consisting of the Dharma, material goods (*āmiṣa*), or skillful means (*kauśala*)— is bestowed upon one who asks or one who does not ask, out of a desire to honor or to benefit them.
Since giving is absent when that [non-giving] exists, it is said to be its opposite.

Avarice (*mātsarya*) is the mental fixation, belonging to the portion of passion, regarding the requisites for life, characterized by an attachment to gain and honor and a desire not to relinquish them.
Its function is to provide a basis for lack of austerity (*asaṃlekha*).
Lack of austerity, moreover, should be understood as the accumulation of requisites—even those not being utilized—due to avarice.
Deceit (*māyā*) is the display of unreal objects for the purpose of deceiving others.
It is the manifestation of things such as moral conduct (*śīla*) in a manner other than they actually exist, by one who is intent on gain and honor and possesses the intention to deceive others.

This is designated based on the conjunction of those two—greed (*rāga*) and delusion (*moha*)—by which one displays non-existent qualities; thus, like anger (*krodha*) and so forth, it exists only as a conceptual designation (*prajñapti*).
It does not exist as a substantial entity;
its function is to provide a basis for wrong livelihood.
Beds, seats, and so forth, acquired through the stratagems of body and speech, are utilized [for this purpose].
And it is not called wrong livelihood because it is obtained through physical exertion.
What is deceit (*śāṭhya*)?
It is the crookedness of the mind comprised of the means for concealing one's own faults.
The means for concealing one's own faults is the deluding of others.
Furthermore, that [deceit] shifts from one thing to another, casts it aside, or proceeds in an unclear manner;
for this very reason, deceit is distinct from concealment (*mrakṣa*),
since the latter conceals only what is already clear.
Crookedness (*vaṅkatā*) is the mental tortuousness that serves as a means for concealing one's own faults; because it is caused by that [concealment],
through its association, the mind does not enter upon the straight path.

And this [concealment of one's faults] is designated as the conjunction of those very two— greed and delusion— by which one, being intent upon gain and honor, acts for the purpose of concealing one's own faults and for the sake of deluding others.
Furthermore, its function is to act as an obstacle to obtaining correct instruction.
It creates an obstacle to that gain which consists in correct instruction and wise attention.
Pride (*mada*) is the exultation of a mind attached to its own prosperity; it is the total absorption [of the mind].
One's own prosperity consists in the excellence of family, health, beauty, youth, strength, sovereignty, intelligence, wisdom, and so forth.
Exultation is a particular kind of joy.
He explains this very specific kind of joy: "the overwhelming of the mind.
By that specific joy through which the mind is rendered independent, it becomes overwhelmed because it is brought under its own control; therefore it is said, "the overwhelming of the mind.
In brief, intoxication (*mada*) is a form of craving accompanied by this specific kind of joy.
And its function is to provide a basis for all primary and secondary afflictions.
Harm (*vihiṃsā*) toward sentient beings consists of various forms of injury, such as killing, binding, beating, and threatening.
It is called "affliction" (*viheṭhanā*) because by means of it—through killing, binding, and so forth—sentient beings are afflicted through the production of physical pain and mental distress.
Furthermore, it is a portion of aversion (*pratigha*), consisting of ruthlessness, lack of compassion, and mercilessness.

Furthermore, these qualities such as cruelty and so forth are to be understood respectively as applying to one who personally commits killing and the like, to one who causes others to do so, and to one who, having seen or heard them being committed by others, approves of them;
or alternatively, they are to be understood through their successive explanations.

This, however, is the summary: *avihiṃsā* (non-harming) is said to be that harshness of mind toward sentient beings which belongs to the portion of hostility (*pratighāṃśika*) and has the function of injuring sentient beings.
"One who has no sense of shame (*hrī*) is called *ahrī* (shameless). That which, through its association with him, is so designated,
and which constitutes the opposite of shame, is *āhrīkya* (lack of shame)."
Even when one perceives oneself as unfit for that action, the lack of shame that persists is *ahrīkya* (shamelessness). That by which one feels abashed is *apatrāpya* (dread of blame).
Lack of moral dread (*anapatrāpya*) is the opposite of that;
it is the absence of shame regarding a sinful action even when one understands: "This which I am doing is contrary to the world and to the scriptures."
It is lack of shame and lack of embarrassment.
Both of these have the function of assisting all primary and secondary afflictions.

Since passion and aversion cannot coexist simultaneously among the various types of passion, aversion, and delusion—which are the causes for the production of the entire view of a self-existent body—they are designated according to their occurrence.
They do not exist independently.
Styāna is the unserviceability of the mind.
He explains it by another synonym: "staimitya. Staimitya is the state of being stiff or motionless (*stimita-bhāva*).
Due to its association with this [state], the mind becomes as if paralyzed through its dullness;
it is no longer able to engage with an object.
Furthermore, this functions as an aid to all primary and secondary afflictions (*kleśa* and *upakleśa*).
And because it is designated within the portion of delusion, it exists only as a designation,
not as a substantial entity.
Excitement (*auddhatya*) is the lack of tranquility of the mind.
For tranquility (*vyupaśama*) is calm abiding (*śamatha*);
its opposite is the lack of tranquility.

Furthermore, that which is conducive to passion—consisting of the recollection of previous laughter, dalliance, play, and so forth—is a cause for the lack of tranquility in the mind as part of passion;
its function is to obstruct calm abiding (*śamatha*).
Regarding "the opposite of faith" (*śraddhā-vipakṣa*):
faith is, respectively, conviction, clarity, and aspiration regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability.
Its opposite—lack of faith—is, conversely, lack of conviction, lack of clarity, and lack of aspiration regarding existence, possession of qualities, and capability.
Its function is to provide a basis for laziness;
because one who lacks faith has no desire for application, it functions to provide a basis for laziness.

Laziness (*kausīdya*) is that lack of mental exertion, which is a part of delusion, occurring with respect to wholesome actions of body, speech, and mind after one has resorted to the pleasure of sleep or reclining on one's side.
One is called "lazy" (*kusīda*) because they sink down (*sīdati*) into what is contemptible (*kutsita*).
The state of that is laziness (*kausīdya*),
which is the opposite of vigor (*vīrya*). Regarding the phrase "the opposite of vigor":
For energy (*vīrya*) is the mental enthusiasm in the application to the side of the wholesome; laziness (*kausīdya*) is its opposite.
And this [laziness] has the function of acting as an obstacle to the application to the side of the wholesome.
Heedlessness (pramāda) is designated with respect to greed, hatred, delusion, and laziness,
as previously explained.
Its function is to provide a basis for the increase of unwholesome states and the decline of wholesome ones.
Lapse of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*) is afflicted mindfulness (*kliṣṭā smṛtiḥ*). "Afflicted" means associated with the afflictions (*kleśa-samprayuktā*).

Regarding the phrase "the failure to express the wholesome": for mindfulness associated with the afflictions is not capable of expressing the wholesome, because it does not have a distinct object from the affliction itself.
And this has the function of providing a basis for distraction.
Distraction (*vikṣepa*) is that by which the mind is scattered in various ways.
Those attachments, aversions, and delusions by which the mind is dispersed outward from the object of meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—
in those cases, distraction is designated as being of the nature of secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*), according to their respective possibilities.
And this has the function of being an obstacle to dispassion.
Lack of clear comprehension (*asamprajanya*) is wisdom associated with the afflictions (*kleśa*),
by means of which one engages in the activities of body, speech, and mind— such as advancing and retreating— without full awareness.
Its function is to provide a basis for transgressions due to ignorance regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) is the mind’s remorse.
That which is done badly is "badly done" (*kukṛta*);
the state of being that is regret (*kaukṛtya*).
Regret (*kaukṛtya*) is said to be a mental distress (*vilekha*) regarding what has been poorly done; this is stated because the context concerns mental factors (*caitasika*).

Having performed or failed to perform what is intended or unintended, wholesome or unwholesome, indeterminate, timely or untimely, appropriate or inappropriate, regret—which is a part of delusion (*moha*)—is the remorse of the mind.
And that is intended [here] as that which is performed preceded by a lack of delight, having the function of being an obstacle to the stability of the mind.
Furthermore, that which is done against one's will by others through forceful restraint, or that which one does due to being overcome by the afflictions (*kleśa*),
lasts as long as time does not cease.
That which is after that time is "untimely.
That which is appropriate is "in place"; that which is inappropriate is "out of place."
And that [ignorance] is also threefold:
wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral;
here, however, that which belongs to the portion of delusion is understood as being comprised within the secondary afflictions (upakleśa).
Drowsiness (*middha*) is a contraction of the mind characterized by a lack of independent functioning.
"Functioning" (*vṛtti*) refers to the engagement with an object;
it is that from which the mind's functioning becomes non-independent.
That is *middha* (torpor);
it is either a state of the mind incapable of sustaining the body or a lack of autonomy [of the mind],
from which that [state] arises.
That is *middha* (torpor).
Since the mind's functioning also becomes independent [of its object] due to other causes, he says: "the contraction of the mind.
He says that the mind's independent functioning consists in the contraction of the mind even due to other causes.
The contraction of the mind is the non-functioning of the sense faculties, such as the eye, through their respective doors.
It is furthermore wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
Depending on the cause of sleepiness—such as attending to signs of weakness, fatigue, heaviness of the body, or darkness—it becomes a part of delusion (*moha*).
Its function is to provide a basis for the failure to perform what ought to be done;
and in this context, it is exclusively unwholesome and a part of delusion,
not anything else.
Vitarka is an investigative mental discourse, a specific form of volition and wisdom.
It is "investigative" because it functions in the mode of examining, [asking] "What is this?
It is "mental discourse" (manojalpa) because it is a discourse whose intrinsic nature is the mind.
"Speech" (*jalpa*) is like verbal expression; it is the articulation of meaning.
It is a specific form of volition (*cetanā*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), because volition consists in the movement of the mind, while wisdom has the aspect of discerning qualities and defects.
Since the activity of the mind occurs under their influence, "applied thought" (*vitarka*) is sometimes designated as both mind and volition.
Sometimes it refers to wisdom (*prajñā*) and volition (*cetanā*), respectively, in their states of deliberation (*abhyūha*) and non-deliberation (*anabhyūha*);
or else, the designation "vitarka" applies to volition and wisdom themselves.
This is because the mind functions in that manner under its influence;
and this same principle should also be understood to apply to investigation (*vicāra*).
Its "coarseness" (*audārikatā*) refers to its grossness, because it has the aspect of searching for the mere object (*vastumātra*).
Investigation (*vicāra*) is a mental discourse that examines,
[determining] "this is that," because it involves the conceptualization (*nirūpaṇa*) of what was previously apprehended.
"In the same way, there is subtlety of mind.
"In the same way" refers to a specific distinction of volition and wisdom;
it is called subtle because, through its mode of searching, it takes the form of examining the object.
These two have as their function providing the basis for dwelling in comfort and discomfort, respectively;
they are distinguished from one another because of their coarse and subtle states of existence.

It has been stated that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) consists of mental factors (*caitasika*) distinct from feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*sañjñā*), as well as formations dissociated from mind (*cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra*).
Among these, the mental factors have already been explained; now the formations dissociated from mind must be discussed. Therefore, he asks: "What are the formations dissociated from mind?"

The definition of those [factors] is stated in general terms, as in the question: "Those which are designated in relation to the states of matter, mind, and mental factors, yet are not designated as being either identical to or different from them, are the dissociated formations (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). This is connected by the context of the treatise.
Because they lack an intrinsic nature distinct from the states of matter and so forth, they are designated in relation to the states of matter and so forth for the sake of conventional usage.

For this very reason, they are not designated as being either identical to or different from their own material cause (*upādāna*), because it would follow that the state and the possessor of the state are either one or many, and because it would follow that the possessor of the state is eternal due to its being an effect.
Since the specific [states] are not understood from the general designation, a question is asked out of a desire to know those specifics: "Which ones, then, are they?"

"Attainment is the attainment of non-perception"— this is a detailed illustration of its specific characteristics. Such categories and such types include whatever else is designated in relation to the states of matter, mind, and mental factors.
These should be understood as formations dissociated from mind.
Furthermore, what are they?
They are: occurrence, determination, conjunction, velocity, sequence, time, place, number, totality, and so forth.
Now, in order to determine the specific nature of each [factor] beginning with "sāmagrī," there is the question: "What is attainment (*prāpti*)? and so forth;
"acquisition (*pratilambha*)" and "possession (*samanvāgama*)" and so forth. It is said that acquisition (*pratilambha*) is the first attainment of something not previously attained.
In the second and subsequent moments of those [dharmas] already acquired, "acquisition" (prāpti) is "possession" (samanvāgama),
because possession is defined as "continuous following" (samanugama).
Thus, it is made known that the word "acquisition" (prāpti) applies both to initial attainment (pratilambha) and to possession (samanvāgama).
Furthermore, that [possession] is divided into three types according to their respective applications: the seed, mastery, and manifestation.

In this regard, the application is as follows: from the first moment onwards, up until the state of mastery, that which is called "attainment" (prāpti) is termed the "seed"; thus, both acquisition (*pratilambha*) and possession (*samanvāgama*) are designated as the seed.
Mastery and manifestation, however, are simply forms of possession (*samanvāgama*).
What, then, is a seed?
A seed is a specific capacity deposited in consciousness by wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral phenomena, which serves as the cause for future phenomena of that same kind.
For when a seed is obtained, because [the result] is dependent upon it, that which has that seed is said to have attained it, even if it has not yet become manifest.

Furthermore, mastery (*vaśitā*) is the state of accomplishing one’s own function without obstruction, depending upon conditions (*pratyaya*). Manifestation (*sammukhībhāva*) is the state of the accomplishment of that function.

The attainment of non-perception (asañjñā-samāpatti) is so called because it is either a non-perception that is an attainment, or the attainment of those who are without perception. "One who is free from passion for the Śubhakṛtsna [heaven]" means one who is free from passion for the third dhyāna;
the third dhyāna consists of the Parīttaśubha [heavens].
the Apramāṇaśubhas and the Śubhakṛtsnas.
Among them, he who is free from passion for the Śubhakṛtsnas—
He is free from passion for the third dhyāna;
"not above" means not above the third dhyāna—
that is, [he is so] while not yet free from passion for the fourth dhyāna.
"Preceded by the perception of deliverance" means that for which mental attention has the perception of deliverance as its precursor is "preceded by the perception of deliverance."

Those who perceive the state of non-perception (*āsañjñika*) as liberation, or who perceive the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) as the path to it, enter the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*).

Therefore, the "perception of escape" (*niḥsaraṇa-saṃjñā*) refers to either the perception of liberation or the perception of its path. In this context, the intended mental attention (*manasikāra*) is that which is preceded by the perception of escape and consists of the aspect of revulsion (*vidūṣaṇākāra*).

For this very reason, even when all mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) have ceased, it is specifically the absence of perception (*saṃjñā*) that is designated as the "attainment of non-perception" (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*).
This is because, by disparaging perception itself, one attains the cessation of all mind and mental factors without exception;
it is the cessation of those unstable minds and mental factors.
The non-abiding [factors] are the six groups of consciousness, together with their associated mental factors, which are comprised within the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
They are called "non-abiding" because they are absent in all states devoid of mind (*acittikāvasthā*), and even in states possessed of mind (*sacittikāvasthā*), they do not exist at all times.
The abiding [factor] is the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) together with its associated mental factors.
Because it exists at all times—

the afflicted mind existing in all states except for the state of meditative attainment of the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga-satya*), the state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), and the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa-avasthā*)— it is said to belong to those that are not stable.

That which is called "cessation" (*nirodha*) is a particular state of the basis (*āśraya*) produced by the mind of meditative attainment, which opposes the continued activity of unstable minds and mental factors for a period of time.
It is called "cessation" because by means of this [state], [the mental factors] are ceased.
Thus, it is stated that the attainment of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) is designated with respect to this particular state of the basis.
That basis which is opposed to the arising of another moment of consciousness immediately after the mind of meditative attainment is said to be "produced by the mind of meditative attainment."

"The attainment of cessation belongs to one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness (*ākiñcanyāyatana*) and has ascended from the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*). Since there is also an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness but has not yet ascended from the peak of existence, he says: "who has ascended from the peak of existence. There is also someone established in the fruit or a candidate for the path who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness but has ascended from the peak of existence; and there is also one who has ascended from the peak of existence but is not yet free from passion for the sphere of nothingness.
Since it might be thought that someone could be both established in the fruit and a candidate for the next stage, he says: "of one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness.

He does not say "one who is not yet free from passion for what is above," because even an Arhat who is free from passion for the peak of existence can attain the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).

By the dual designation "one who is free from passion for the sphere of nothingness" and "one who has set out from the peak of existence," it is made known that this attainment belongs only to a noble one— either a non-returner or an arhat— and not to an ordinary person;
for an ordinary person does not set out from the peak of existence.
Because there is no path that serves as an antidote to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*),
whereas the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) is an antidote to the peak of existence and the uncontaminated path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) is also [an antidote],
it is only an noble one (*ārya*) who has departed from the peak of existence.

And having become dispassionate through the abandonment of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision, one enters [the attainment] with a mental attention preceded by the perception of dwelling; for they do not enter the attainment of cessation with a mental attention preceded by the perception of deliverance— as they do in the case of the attainment of non-perception— but rather with a mental attention preceded by the perception of dwelling.
The attainment of cessation belongs to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*); however, the notion of renunciation regarding existence does not arise for the noble ones (*ārya*).

Because they are weary of perception and feeling, and because those [perceptions and feelings] are absent in the attainment of cessation, they possess the notion of a peaceful dwelling within that attainment of cessation.
"Abiding" (vihāra) is the designation "abiding"; or, it is called an abiding because one abides by means of it.
The meaning is that one passes the interval of time by means of it.

The mental attention conditioned by the notion, "We shall dwell in a distinguished meditative attainment that resembles nirvāṇa," is called the mental attention preceded by the notion of dwelling. Furthermore, this is subtle and belongs to the peak of existence (*bhavāgra*), because immediately after it, the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) becomes manifest.

Regarding the phrase "of the non-stable," this refers to the cessation of six active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*)—four, one, and [the sixth] respectively—as they enter meditative absorption in the desire, form, and formless realms.
Regarding the phrase "and of some of the stable":
since there are also those included within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) that are called "stable," he says "of some" to specify them.

Furthermore, because the afflicted mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) has the nature of abiding throughout all states involving outflows (*sāsrava*), it is characterized by stability, except during the state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) and the stage of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).

"Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to the impairment of the seeds of the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the afflicted mind within the resultant consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*), brought about by the meditative attainment.
It is called "cessation" because by means of this [attainment], the evolving consciousnesses and the afflicted mind are suppressed so that they do not arise for a period of time.

And thus, when the state of the seeds of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) has been impaired by the mind of meditative attainment, the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is designated.

Non-perception (*āsañjñika*) is the fruit of the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*); it is the cessation of unstable mental states and mental factors for one reborn among the gods who are beings without perception. The gods called Bṛhatphala constitute the third distinct location within the fourth *dhyāna*.
Above them, like a separate enclosure, is the abode of the gods who are beings without perception.
For one born there, the fruit of maturation (*vipākaphala*) is the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñi-samāpatti*).
Its essential nature is defined as the cessation of unstable minds and mental factors (*citta-caitta*).

For in that state, the unstable minds and mental factors of one who has been reborn there arise in an increasingly diminished state while they exist upon their own basis, causing the seeds of minds and mental factors of their own kind to be impaired.
Until finally, having reached a state of extreme exhaustion, they are unable to connect with another moment of mind because the seeds within their own basis have been impaired; consequently,
the unstable minds and mental factors do not arise at that time due to the absence of such a basis.
And when that basis is in the state of having its seeds impaired, the "unconscious" (āsañjñika) is designated for it.
Thus, it is precisely a particular state of the basis that is called "cessation" (nirodha), because by this [state], [the mind and mental factors] are ceased.

The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) is the determination of the duration of the existence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a particular homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*), projected by prior karma.
It is called "life" (*jīvita*) because one lives by means of it;
it is a faculty (*indriya*) precisely because it exercises sovereignty over the persistence of that homogeneous class.
*Nikāya* means a collection of sentient beings.
*Sabhāga* means having a common portion (*samāno bhāgaḥ*), which signifies being similar (*sadṛśa*).
They are the homogeneous groups (nikāyasabhāga).
