Within those homogeneous groups, which are differentiated by the distinction of destinies and the distinction of karma, that continuum of aggregates belonging to a single birth for each individual is designated as the "homogeneous group" (nikāyasabhāga).

That which is called the "determination of the duration of stay" is the production of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) comprised within a homogeneous class (nikāyasabhāga) that has not yet been differentiated; it is produced by karma and pierced by the karma previously accumulated—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or imperturbable (āneñjya). This is what is meant by the determination of the duration of stay.

The determination of the duration of that stability is the rule for the time of its endurance, such as: "By this [being], one must remain in this homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) for this much time—for a hundred years or a thousand years.
Thus, it is said that life-force (*āyus*) has the nature of a determined period of stability.

Its basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), however, consists of the stable conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) preceded by the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which possess a specific capacity projected by karma accumulated in a previous birth.

The "homogeneity of group" (nikāyasabhāga) is the commonality of the personal existence (ātmabhāva) among sentient beings. Sentient beings are those included within the five destinies, such as gods, humans, and so forth.
It is that wherein their state of being "self" (ātman) resides.

That is the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of sentient beings; furthermore, it consists of the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) or the four aggregates. Homogeneity (*sabhāgatā*) is similarity.

This is what is meant: for sentient beings who are differentiated by distinctions such as destiny (*gati*), station (*sthāna*), and personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), there is a mutual similarity of personal existence among them based upon those very distinctions of destiny, station, and personal existence; therein is the designation "homogeneity of class" (*nikāyasabhāga*).
Birth (*jāti*) is the coming-into-being of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within that homogeneity of class where they previously did not exist.

The mention of "homogeneity of the group" (nikāyasabhāga) indicates that birth is not the arising of mere conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) in general; rather, birth is the coming-into-being of those very conditioned phenomena that exist within a particular homogeneity of the group,
after having previously not existed.
This is for the purpose of making it known that [this does not apply] to all [entities].

In order to refute the opinion of those who maintain that entities which have neither arisen nor perished possess a "birth" (*jāti*) as a distinct entity (*arthāntarabhūtā*) and that the establishment of the time-periods (*adhvan*) is based on causal activity (*kāritra*), he says: "existence after having not existed" (*abhūtvā bhāvaḥ*).
For birth (*jāti*) is simply the coming into being of the conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) themselves after not having existed;
it is not a separate entity, nor is the establishment of the time-periods (*adhvan*) based on causal activity (*kāritra*).

[Page 83] Aging (*jarā*) is likewise the transformation of the continuity (*prabandhānyathātva*) of those very [conditioned phenomena]. "Of those very ones" refers specifically to the conditioned phenomena included within a homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*). "Transformation of the continuity" refers to the period from the existence at birth (*upapattibhava*) until the existence at death (*maraṇabhava*).
In that context, the continuous arising of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) existing in the relationship of cause and effect is called a "continuum" (*prabandha*).
Its becoming otherwise and otherwise is "alteration" (*anyathātva*).
For instance, it proceeds from the stage of the *kalala* to the stage of the *arbuda*, and so on, up to the stage of old age.

Even in states such as the *kalala* and so forth, one must state that there is a moment-by-moment alteration of the subsequent [state] from the preceding one. Thus, the designation "aging" refers to the alteration of the continuum (*prabandha*),
neither to a single moment nor to something that exists as a separate entity.
"Abiding" (*sthiti*) is likewise the continuation of their stream (*prabandhānuvṛtti*).
"Likewise" means within a single homogeneous class of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*);
it is a designation for the abiding that consists in the continuous occurrence of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) until death.
It is thereby made known that [the continuum] is neither a single moment nor something distinct from it.
Their impermanence is likewise the cessation of the continuum.
"Theirs likewise" means that impermanence is designated when the continuum of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within a single homogeneous class (*nikāyasabhāga*) ceases;
it does not occur at every moment, nor is it something that exists as a separate entity.
In this context, death should be understood as the cessation of the continuity [of the stream].
Now, since external matter (*rūpa*) also possesses birth, aging, duration, and impermanence,
for what reason are birth and the other characteristics said to belong only to the stream of conditioned factors (*saṃskāra-santāna*) within the homogeneous class (*nikāya-sabhāga*)?
"Not of external form" means that these characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) which were spoken of by the Blessed One— namely, birth, aging, duration, and impermanence—
are intended with reference only to those formations (*saṃskāra*) designated as sentient beings, and not to external ones; this is for the purpose of making this known.

But why did the Blessed One, although both [internal and external phenomena] are equal in their nature as born entities (*jātisattva*), teach the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛtalakṣaṇa*) with reference only to appropriated (*upātta*) formations?
For external form is characterized by evolution and dissolution (*saṃvarta-vivarta*),
whereas internal formations are characterized by birth, aging, and so forth.

This is what is meant: the destruction and arising of external form are well-known in the world by the terms *saṃvarta* (dissolution) and *vivarta* (evolution); thus, the Blessed One, conforming to worldly convention, spoke of them in that very way, and not by means of terms such as "birth" (*jāti*) and so forth.

However, internal conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are characterized by birth, aging, and so on—being born, aged, persisting, and perished—and therefore, even by the Blessed One, their arising and so forth were designated by terms such as "birth" and so forth, in conformity with worldly usage.
Thus it is said.

The name-group (*nāmakāya*) consists of designations for the intrinsic nature of phenomena. It is called "name" (*nāma*) because it bends (*namayati*) cognition toward each respective object of expression (*abhidheya*). Furthermore, it is a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*) whose limits have been established with respect to meanings.
A collection of names or phonemes is a name-body (*nāmakāya*).
Since the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) of phenomena cannot be expressed, speech that applies [words] to it is "designation" (*adhivacana*).
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).
That by which the intrinsic nature of phenomena— which are themselves inexpressible— is illuminated is called a designation (*abhidhāna*) or a name (*nāman*);
for example, "eye," "ear," "form," or "sound."

The phrase-body (*padakāya*) consists of the specific designations for phenomena. It is called a "phrase" (*pada*) because by means of it, a meaning together with its specific qualities is traversed (*padyate*).
In this way, the phrase is distinguished from both the name (*nāman*) and the worldly phrase.

Although there is no difference between a name (*nāman*) and a phrase (*pada*) in that both consist of a collection of phonemes (*varṇa*), they are distinguished by their specific meanings: a "name" is a designation for the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, while a "phrase" is a designation for their specific qualities (*viśeṣa*).
Since a specific quality has the intrinsic nature as its basis, the designation of the intrinsic nature comes first.

Furthermore, a particularity (*viśeṣa*) is that which consists of both conformity and exclusion; it is called a "particularity" because it distinguishes an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that does not recur elsewhere, such as: "All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent."
"All phenomena are without self;
nirvana is peace.
What is meant by this is that a name is merely a designation for the intrinsic nature of a thing.
A "phrase" (pada) is the designation of the intrinsic nature of a qualified object;
the remainder, however, is to be understood from the explanation of "name" (nāman).
The collection of phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) refers to the syllables (*akṣara*), based on their function as the manifesters of both [meaning and phonemes].
It is called a "phoneme" (*vyañjana*) because it manifests (*vyajyate*) by means of this.
The collection of phonemes is the "collection of phonemes" (*vyañjanakāya*).
The inclusion of the word "body" (kāya) is for the purpose of including all phonemes (vyañjana). From the word "that" (tat) alone, one might suspect it refers only to what immediately precedes it;
from the word "both" (ubhaya) alone, it would not be known which "both" is intended.

Therefore, the designation "both" refers to those two together. Thus, because they manifest both the name and the phrase immediately following [the phonemes], they are called "manifesters" (*vyañjana*). But how, then, do the phonemes (*akṣara*) manifest names and phrases?
When syllables have come together and reached the state of being designated as specific intrinsic natures (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*), they constitute names and phrases through such designation.
Thus, while syllables manifest names and phrases, the syllables themselves do not have the nature of vocal intimation (*vāg-vijñapti*).
It is well known in the world that [syllables] such as *a* and so forth are "phonemes" (*varṇa*).
Furthermore, they are called "phonemes" (varṇa) because they describe the meaning by serving as the basis for names and phrases.
Since names and phrases are designated only for objects in whatever state those objects have been analyzed, they are said to be the basis for them.
Furthermore, their "unchanging nature" (*akṣaratva*) is based on the fact that they do not undergo change (*akṣaraṇa*) among synonyms.
For instance, the term "eye" (*cakṣus*) changes when other synonyms such as "netrā" and so forth are used;
the meaning is that it is understood through other synonyms by virtue of being the object of expression.
Furthermore, there is no other synonym for the letter *a* by which the letter *a* could be understood apart from its actual designation as *a*.
And all that there is is this: namely, [the following].
Intrinsic nature, specific difference, and the conventional usage of both—

since all of these are conventionally expressed by means of these [three], the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes are thus established. In this same way, it should be understood that the other dissociated factors are also established in view of their respective purposes, just like the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes.

Ordinariness (*pṛthagjanatva*) is the non-attainment of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). That dharma through the connection with which one is designated as an "ordinary person" (*pṛthagjana*) is ordinariness.
They are called "Noble Ones" (ārya) because they have gone far away from evil, unwholesome states.
They, moreover, are those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Their dharmas are the paths of seeing, cultivation, and no-more-training.
The non-attainment of these is the state of being an ordinary person (*pṛthagjanatva*).

Furthermore, "non-attainment" here refers to the non-arising of the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*). For it is said that a continuum of sentient beings in whom the noble dharmas have not arisen is an ordinary person.
But one is called "noble" (ārya) because of the arising of the noble dharmas.
What is "proceeding" (pravṛtti)?
The non-interruption of the continuity of cause and fruit is called proceeding;
the designation "proceeding" does not apply to a single moment or to the cessation of the continuity.
What is specific determination (*pratiniyama*)? It is the establishment of specific determination based on the diversity of causes and fruits.
Furthermore, the diversity of causes and fruits consists of virtuous conduct for a desired object.
"Bad conduct is the cause of what is undesirable," and so forth; thus, the various fruits have distinct, mutually independent causes.
What is yoga?
It is the designation for the conformity between cause and fruit.
For example, it is appropriate to say that the perfection of wealth is the result of giving; thus, the perfection of wealth is the fruit of giving.
What is speed?
It is the designation "speed" for the rapid occurrence of cause and effect.
What is sequential order (*anukrama*)?
It is a designation for the occurrence of causes and fruits one by one. Occurrence one by one is non-simultaneous occurrence.
[88] What is time? Time is a designation for the continuous progression of the causal series.
When there is a continuous progression of cause and effect, that which therein is the cause and effect that has arisen and ceased—
That which has passed is designated as "past time";
that which has not yet arisen is "future";
and that which has arisen but not yet ceased is "present time."
What is space?
Space is a designation for the cause and the fruit themselves in all ten directions—east, south, west, north, below, above, and so forth.
The conventional term "space" is applied to the extension of the cause and the fruit throughout the various directions.
And cause and effect should be understood as being comprised within form,
because that which is formless lacks the capacity to pervade space.
What is number?
It is a designation for the differentiation of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra) one by one.
Differentiation is so called because, if there were an undifferentiated single essence, a second number would be impossible.
What is the totality?
It is a designation for the coming together of causes and conditions.

Thus, these formations dissociated from mind (cittaviprayukta-saṃskāra) should be understood as existing only as designations (prajñaptisat), being conceptually established upon specific states of phenomena.
The aggregate of formations has been explained.
Immediately after the aggregate of formations, the aggregate of consciousness is to be understood; therefore, he asks: "What is the aggregate of consciousness? [He replies:
"It is the representation of the object."
The object of focus (*ālambana*) is the domain of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). It, moreover, is of six kinds: from form (*rūpa*) up to phenomena (*dharma*).
Its "representation" (vijñapti) means grasping, comprehension, or apprehension.
Furthermore, that consists of the six evolving consciousnesses,
from eye-consciousness up to mind-consciousness.
In this context, visual consciousness is the discernment of visible forms based upon the visual faculty;
likewise, up to mental consciousness, which is the discernment of all phenomena based upon the mental faculty.
Having stated the essential nature of consciousness (*vijñāna*), he says— in order to demonstrate its synonyms— "That is also called mind (*citta*) and intellect (*manas*).
That consciousness is also termed "mind," and it is also termed "intellect."
To demonstrate the meaning of these synonyms, he says: "by taking up variety and by taking up its dependence upon the mind.
By taking up variety, it is called *citta*;
by taking up its dependence upon the immediately preceding mind (*samanantaracitta*), it is called *manas*.

In this regard, because the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) has the nature of discerning its object, and because the discernment of the object possesses manifold aspects, the visual and other consciousnesses arise as variegated. For this very reason, although it arises by depending upon the sense faculties (*indriya*), it is said that "it cognizes the object," and not that it cognizes the faculty.

Likewise, among the six consciousnesses—eye-consciousness and the rest—that which ceases serves as the basis for the immediately succeeding consciousness that is arising; therefore, by virtue of being the support for the immediately preceding mind (*samanantaracitta*), it is called "mind" (*manas*).
That which was described as "mind" because of its variegated nature, [is now so designated in this sense].
This refers to the genus (*jāti*),
not to the specific characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*).
However, because a specific characteristic has a fixed object and mode of apprehension (*ālambanākāra*) and is thus not manifold (*citra*), it is not "mind" (*citta*) in the primary sense.
Furthermore, with respect to preeminence, "mind" (*citta*) refers to the *ālayavijñāna*.
He states the reason for this very point: "For it is accumulated (*cita*) with the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*).
Because it is accumulated moment by moment with the seeds of all conditioned phenomena, it is called "mind"; thus, that alone is the mind in its primary sense.
Accumulation (*caya*), however, is the repeated nourishment of the seed, or the continuous succession of the seeds of formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
Here, "formative forces" refers to contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*);
their re-arising occurs from four conditions.

In this context, the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) is the latent impression (*vāsanā*) residing within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) manifest repeatedly, the nourishment of the seeds is called "latent impression.
The dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) consists of the sense faculties, such as the eye and so forth.
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is consciousness that has just ceased.
The objective condition (*ālambanapratyaya*) consists of form and so forth.
For it is also said in the Sūtra: "The eye is unimpaired... [p. 91]
When visible forms have come into range and the corresponding mental attention is present, thus there occurs the manifestation of the visual consciousness born thereof.
The same should be stated for the consciousnesses of the ear and so forth, as applicable.
However, the causal conditions are not mentioned because they are always present and because they are difficult to discern.
Immediately following that is the investigative mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
Immediately after the investigative [consciousness] arises the determining [consciousness],
and likewise, immediately after the determining [consciousness], the conceptualizing mental consciousness arises;
therein, one is either defiled or purified on account of the object.
In that state, one performs meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formative forces (*saṃskāra*) consisting of volition (*cetanā*).

When these have been performed and are ceasing, they nourish either the maturation-habit-energy (*vipākavāsanā*) or the outflow-habit-energy (*niṣyandavāsanā*) within the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Therein, based upon the outflow-habit-energy, meritorious, non-meritorious, and imperturbable formative forces proceed from the storehouse-consciousness.

Depending upon the latencies of maturation (*vipākavāsanā*), from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) itself, a storehouse consciousness that is of the nature of maturation is produced within other homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*).
In this regard, the same principle applies to those other phenomena that are unwholesome (*akuśala*) and wholesome-with-outflows (*kuśalasāsrava*).
However, neutral (*avyākṛta*) phenomena nourish only the latencies of outflow (*niṣyandavāsanā*).
It does not [contain] the latencies of maturation,
because those are not of the nature of maturation.
Thus, the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is of two kinds.
Based on the perfuming of the outflow (*niṣyanda-vāsanā*), there is both effect and cause.

For all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), while existing in the implantation of their own seeds, are established as the cause for the excellence of the nature of the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); thus, the storehouse-consciousness is the effect of all conditioned phenomena.

And since all conditioned phenomena arise from the storehouse-consciousness by taking its seeds as their appropriation (*upādāna*), the storehouse-consciousness is the cause of all conditioned phenomena.

However, with respect to the maturation-impression (*vipākavāsanā*), that [resultant consciousness] is solely the effect of wholesome and unwholesome formative forces (*saṃskāra*), not their cause. But as for its cause, it is the resultant consciousness itself within other homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), based upon that maturation-impression.

For the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), because it takes form, sound, and so forth as its objects and because it possesses the aspects of specific and general characteristics, has delimited objects and delimited aspects.
The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), however, has undelimited objects and aspects;
for its object cannot be delimited.
It is not a mode [of perception].
What is the reason?
Because the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) proceeds by means of two kinds of objects.
Internally, it consists of the representation of appropriation (*upādāna-vijñapti*),
and externally, it consists of the representation of the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) in its undifferentiated form.

Therein, internal appropriation refers to the latencies (*vāsanā*) of adherence to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), as well as the material sense-faculties together with their physical bases (*sādhiṣṭhāna-indriya-rūpa*).

And because this object of focus is subtle, it is difficult even for worldly scholars to comprehend; therefore, it is said to have an "unascertained object and aspect," yet it is not that it is entirely without an object.
The evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) belongs to the categories of wholesome, afflicted, and neutral, whereas the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) belongs to a single category.
In that regard, it is first of all not of the nature of wholesome or unwholesome, because it is not associated with wholesome or unwholesome [mental factors].
For it is associated only with the five omnipresent mental factors (*sarvatraga-caitasika*).

Because it has as its cause the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) of prior karma, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), together with its associated mental factors—namely attention, contact, feeling, perception, and volition—is exclusively a maturation (*vipāka*); thus, it is of an exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature.

Furthermore, the continuity of the stream here refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, which, having taken up rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) in various homogeneous classes of beings (*nikāyasabhāga*), proceeds as a flow of momentary succession from that point until death;
it is not interrupted at intervals like the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).
For instance, immediately after visual consciousness, auditory and other consciousnesses arise.
Immediately after auditory consciousness, visual and other consciousnesses arise;
likewise, immediately after olfactory and other consciousnesses, and so forth, it should be stated in detail.
Similarly, an unwholesome state arises immediately after a wholesome one.
After the unwholesome, the wholesome arises;
after both of those, the neutral arises;
and after that which belongs to a lower realm, that which belongs to a middle realm arises.
Immediately after a medium realm comes a sublime realm; immediately after a sublime realm comes a non-sublime realm;
and immediately after a non-sublime realm comes a medium realm—this should be stated in detail.
Nor does a single substance persist until death.
How is it known that there exists an *ālayavijñāna* distinct from the six types of evolving consciousness? It is known both through scripture (*āgama*) and through reasoning (*yukti*).
Regarding scripture: it was stated by the Blessed One in the *Abhidharmasūtra*: "The element (*dhātu*) is beginningless; it is the common support of all phenomena."
When that exists, all states of existence as well as the attainment of nirvāṇa exist.
Furthermore, it is also stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*: "The appropriating consciousness (*ādānavijñāna*), profound and subtle, flows like a torrent containing all seeds;
I have not revealed this to the foolish, lest they should imagine it to be a self."

He also speaks with reference to logical reasoning (*yukti*): because the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*), known as the representation of objects, arises again for one who has emerged from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), and the state of non-perception (*āsañjñika*), that [consciousness] is the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) which is a distinct entity from the active consciousnesses; this is the completion of the sentence.

For one who has entered the attainment of cessation or the attainment of non-perception, or when the state of non-perception has manifested, all active consciousnesses have ceased without remainder; yet, at the time of emerging again, [the active consciousness would arise] without the storehouse-consciousness—[which is logically impossible].
The arising of the active consciousnesses is not tenable;
for it is not logical that they arise from the mind of meditative attainment,
because that [attainment-mind] has long since ceased, and what has ceased is non-existent.

And that which is non-existent is neither an effect nor a cause, like the *pradhāna*, the self (*ātman*), and so forth. As for one who thinks: "The essential nature of an entity is devoid of loss, acquisition, or modification; rather, the future, present, and past states of entities are determined by way of their causal activity (*kāritra*)."
For it is said that the future is that which has not yet performed its activity,
the present is that which is performing its activity,
and the past is that which has ceased its activity.
If that is so, then one must admit that activity (kāritra) is distinct from the entity (bhāva), because the entity is admitted to exist even when activity is absent in its past and future states.
And thus, it is the activity itself that has arising and passing away,
not the entities.
Because of arising after not having existed and ceasing after having existed,
[the self does not exist] in form, sensation, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, since these are always superimposed with their own intrinsic natures.
Furthermore, because there would be an absence of arising and passing away, the aggregates such as form and so forth would not be impermanent, just like cessation;
and consequently, they would not even be suffering.
For it is said in the Sūtra: "That which is impermanent is suffering."
And for one who contemplates the aggregates in this way as impermanent and suffering, there would indeed be a cognitive distortion (*viparyāsa*).
Yet, it is not logical that the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśaprahāṇa*) occurs through a cognitive distortion,
just as [it is not logical] that there is the distortion of permanence and pleasure regarding what is impermanent and suffering.
Furthermore, because activity possesses both arising and ceasing, it would follow that it is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
and since it is not included among the aggregates of form and so forth, a sixth aggregate would have to be admitted.

Moreover, one could not say that all contaminated (*sāsrava*) phenomena are subsumed under the aggregates of clinging (*upādānaskandha*), or that all conditioned phenomena are subsumed under the [five] aggregates.
Another, however, says: "Activity" (*kāritra*) means the grasping of a fruit.

For when one dharma stands as the causal state for another dharma, that [first] dharma grasps that [second] dharma as its fruit; therefore, the establishment of the causal state of entities is the grasping of a fruit.
And since that very dharma is established as the cause, activity is not other than the dharmas;
therefore, the fault mentioned immediately above does not follow.
For that which is "not other" is indeed that very same thing.
This is what is meant: activity is not something other than the phenomenon;
rather, the phenomenon itself is the activity.
Likewise, the phenomenon is not something other than the activity.
If activity itself is the dharma,
then in this way, in the past and future time-periods, there would be an absence of dharma just as there is an absence of activity;
consequently, the doctrine of the existence of the past and future would be abandoned.
Alternatively, since activity (kāritra) is not distinct from the dharma itself—just as the nature of the dharma is not—it must be admitted that activity belongs to the three time periods.
Even so, the doctrine that "the time periods are established by means of activity" is abandoned;
for it is accepted that what is performing activity is the present.
Furthermore, one thing is produced by another,
not by itself,
because it has already been produced.
And that which was not done is being done, not that which has already been done;
therefore, because of the state of being done or not done, there is clearly a difference between the dharma and its activity.
Therefore, the previously mentioned fault remains exactly as it was.
Furthermore, if the dharma and its activity were non-different, it would follow that there is no relationship between cause and effect;
for since the effect would already be fully established prior [to the activity], just like the cause, what could the cause do for the effect? Thus, how could it be a cause?
Or how can that which does not act be a cause? Furthermore, how can an effect, being produced by that [cause], be its result if it is not itself produced by it?
Moreover, the relationship of cause and effect exists only among activities (*kāritra*) themselves.
Not of phenomena;
for when activity exists, another activity arises,
but not when it does not exist.
But it is not the intrinsic nature of a dharma, nor does the intrinsic nature of a dharma arise from the intrinsic nature of a dharma,
because it exists at all times.
And thus, that in the presence of which something comes to be, and in the absence of which it does not come to be,
is the cause of that thing, and the other is the effect.
This is well-known in the world;

and thus, [if one were to claim] that the intrinsic nature of a phenomenon (*dharmasvarūpa*) is neither cause nor effect, there would be a contradiction with both worldly convention and the treatises.
Others maintain that the activity (*kāritra*) of a phenomenon is inexpressible as being either identical to or different from its reality (*tattva*).
For what reason is it not expressible as being identical? Because it does not possess the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.
For what reason is it not expressed as being different?
It is not even said to be "other," because it does not possess the nature of another either.
If that is so, then that which possesses neither its own nature nor the nature of another must simply be non-existent, like the horn of a hare, due to its lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*).
How can that which does not exist serve as the basis for the establishment of the time-periods?
Thus, the establishment of the time-periods cannot be proven in any way through functional activity (*kāritra*).
Therefore, an entity that has not yet arisen is the future.
It must be accepted that what has ceased is the past, and what has arisen but not yet ceased is the present;
however, the future is not that which does not perform its activity.
That which performs its activity is present;
that whose activity has ceased is past.

Another, however, says: "Matter with its sense-faculties and the mind are mutual seeds"; therefore, for one emerging from the attainment of cessation, the attainment of non-perception, or the state of non-perception, the mind arises from matter with its sense-faculties.
Just as, for one passing away from the formless realm, matter with its sense-faculties arises from the mind alone, even though it had been ceased for a long time.
Therefore, there is no need here for the *ālayavijñāna*.
If that were the case, then each individual sentient being would have two mental continua (*cittasantāna*):
one from the physical form together with the sense faculties (*sendriya-rūpa*), and [the other from the mind].
Furthermore, [the mind] is other than the consciousness;
moreover, in the formless realms, for one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation, there is an absence of form and thus an absence of emergence from that state.
Consequently, it would follow that such a person would simply attain final nirvana [without ever emerging]; therefore, this must not be so conceived.
Furthermore, a single cause is held to be characterized by its own existence, effortless, impermanent, and capable—not the opposite.
For it was said by the Blessed One: "When this exists, that comes to be."
"From the arising of this, that arises;
namely, conditioned by ignorance are the formative forces.
Therefore, the cause is not eternal.
Nor is it non-existent, nor is it devoid of activity, nor is it incapable;

for the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is accompanied by the seeds of all conditioned phenomena and persists as a continuum until death. Thus, for one emerging from a state of mindlessness, the active consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arises precisely from the storehouse consciousness.
Regarding the statement "it arises," the Sūtra also says: "The consciousness of one who has entered the attainment of cessation has not departed from the body.
Furthermore, it is not logical that any consciousness other than the ālayavijñāna should remain non-departed from the body during the state of the attainment of cessation.
What is the reason?

If it is maintained that for one who has attained the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), there is the manifestation of a consciousness other than the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*),

then— given the statement in the Sūtra that "contact (*sparśa*) is the coming together of the three, and feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*) are born together with contact"— it must also be admitted that perception and feeling manifest as well.
Furthermore, because feeling (*vedanā*) and perception (*sañjñā*) would still exist, there could be no cessation of perception and feeling (*sañjñā-vedita-nirodha*) at all.
As for the one who thinks: "In the Sūtra it is stated that craving (*tṛṣṇā*) has feeling as its condition, yet not every feeling is a condition for craving"—[this is incorrect].
In this way, it is not the case that every contact (*sparśa*) is a condition for perception and feeling (*saṃjñā-vedanā*); thus, there is no fault [in our position].
But this is not so; for in another sutra, feeling is specified: "Craving arises dependent on the felt (*vedita*) born from contact with ignorance (*avidyā-saṃsparśaja*)."
But contact has never been qualified in such a manner; therefore, this case is not the same.

Consequently, one must necessarily admit that from the *ālayavijñāna* alone—which contains all seeds and persists as a continuum in all states—the mind that emerges from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*), and the state of non-perception (*asañjñika*) arises.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is distinct from the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) on account of its dependence upon objective conditions (*ālambanapratyaya*) and its occurrence in a different mode.
The word "on account of" (*upādāya*), which is indicated at the end [of the previous section], is also connected here.
The objective condition for the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, consists of the five objects, such as visible form.
For mental consciousness, all phenomena are its objects.
From the aspect of form and so forth, the aspect of sound and so forth is a different mode;
likewise, from the aspect of sound and so forth, the aspect of form and so forth [is another].
The aspect of blue and so forth is a different mode from the aspect of yellow and so forth;
thus it should be stated in detail for all cases.
Since the occurrence of this consciousness—the acquisition of its own nature—is by way of a different mode, that consciousness is "occurring in a different mode" (*prakārāntaravṛtti*).

Its state is the occurrence in another mode. That occurrence in another mode has dependence on the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) as its cause; thus, it is "that which has dependence on the object-condition" for the occurrence in another mode.

By taking up—that is, by grasping—such a state of functioning in a different mode, it is understood that there exists an *ālayavijñāna* distinct from the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which serves as the seed for those evolving consciousnesses.

For in this context, consciousness is differentiated from one another due to differences in their objective manifestations, not due to differences in the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) or the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Therefore, it has been stated thus: "by taking up the state of functioning in a different mode in dependence upon the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)."
And just as that occurrence in another mode is not tenable if it were independent of an objective support (*ālambana*),
so too it is not at all tenable if it were independent of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
And whatever [being] is permeated by the seeds of certain [phenomena],...
That [ālayavijñāna] is their cause and condition.

Furthermore, it is not logical for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) to serve as seeds for one another, because these consciousnesses—whether wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral; belonging to the inferior, intermediate, or superior realms; mundane or supramundane; and with-outflows (*sāsrava*) or without-outflows (*anāsrava*)—occur only successively.

For it is not observed that a latent impression (*vāsanā*) is produced by that very same [entity], nor by another that is either at a different time or unconnected; rather, the impression of sesame seeds and the like is observed precisely through flowers and the like arising and perishing simultaneously with them.

Therefore, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), which arise from and perish along with the ripening-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*) at the same time, render that ripening-consciousness capable of producing an effect corresponding to themselves.
Its capacity is called "latency" (*vāsanā*).

It must necessarily be admitted that from the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*), which has been perfumed by those various modes of active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*), there arise again active consciousnesses that depend upon objects and function in various ways as wholesome, unwholesome, and so forth.

And thus, it is established that the maturation-consciousness (vipākavijñāna), which is accompanied by the seeds of all conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛtadharma), is distinct from the active consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna).

Furthermore, because there is a recurrence after being interrupted, it should be understood that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists as something distinct from the active consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*).

In states such as mindless sleep or fainting, when the continuum of the active consciousnesses has been interrupted, the arising of active consciousnesses once again upon the departure of that mindless sleep or fainting would not be possible without the storehouse consciousness.
In this case as well, an investigation should be conducted, similar to that regarding the mind emerging from the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and other states.
And with reference to the engagement in and the cessation of saṃsāra:
the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is distinct from the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna),
for it is understood that the engagement in and the cessation of saṃsāra have that [storehouse-consciousness] as their cause.

The arising of the aggregates of clinging through a continuous succession of moments, states, and homogeneous classes is called *saṃsāra*. Its further progression consists in the rebirth-linking (*pratisandhi*) into other homogeneous classes;
its cessation consists in the realm of nirvana with remainder and the realm of nirvana without remainder.

In that regard, if the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is not accepted, the progression of saṃsāra is not tenable because of the absence of a consciousness conditioned by formative forces (*saṃskāra*).
For if the storehouse consciousness is not accepted, one would have to imagine either the consciousness at rebirth (*pratisandhivijñāna*) as being conditioned by formative forces,
or the six groups of consciousness permeated by formative forces as being the consciousness conditioned by formative forces.
In that regard, the consciousness at rebirth does not have the formative forces accumulated in a previous birth as its condition,
because the formative forces accumulated in a previous birth have long since ceased,
and what has ceased is non-existent.
And because there is no causal condition for that which is non-existent;
if it is not accepted that what has ceased can function as a causal condition, then,
this being the case, action would be entirely fruitless.
For the maturation does not arise from a present action;
this is not so,
because of the persistence of the cultivation produced by it.
The maturation arises from a latent impression (*vāsanā*) deposited by an action within the mental continuum that has reached a specific state of ripening;
therefore, action is not fruitless,
nor does maturation arise from an action that has already ceased.
And at the moment of rebirth-linking, it is name-and-form itself [that arises],
not consciousness alone;
therein, consciousness alone has the formative forces as its condition.
And what is the reasoning here for [the claim] that it is not name-and-form?
Therefore, it should be stated that name-and-form has formations as its condition, and not consciousness.
Or what else is "name-and-form conditioned by consciousness" other than that which occurs after the moment of rebirth-linking?
What specific distinction does it possess over the name-and-form at the moment of rebirth-linking, such that only this [subsequent state] is conditioned by consciousness and not the former?

Furthermore, if the former [consciousness] has the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its condition and the subsequent one does not, then let name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) itself have the formative forces as its condition.
What is the use of postulating the linking consciousness (*pratisandhivijñāna*) as a separate member?
Therefore, it is not logical that the linking consciousness has the formative forces as its condition.
The formative forces (saṃskāra), however, have ignorance as their condition;
and consciousness (vijñāna) perfumed by them has the formative forces as its condition;
and with that as its condition, there is name-and-form (nāmarūpa) at the moment of rebirth-linking—this alone is the faultless principle.
The position that the six groups of consciousness, permeated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*), constitute "consciousness conditioned by formative forces" is also untenable.
Why?
Because consciousness is not capable of depositing within itself either the latencies of maturation (*vipākavāsanā*) or the latencies of outflow (*niṣyandavāsanā*).
Because there is a contradiction in the self performing its own activity; nor [is it the case] with respect to the immediately preceding [moment],
because that has not yet arisen at that time, and what has not arisen lacks existence.
Nor does it exist when [the mind] has already arisen, because at that time the preceding [moment] has ceased;

furthermore, in mindless states such as those of sleep and so forth, since the arising of a mind permeated by formative forces (*saṃskāra*) would be impossible, name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) conditioned by consciousness (*vijñāna*) would not exist.

In the absence of that [consciousness], the six sense bases would not exist; likewise, everything up to old age and death would not exist. Consequently, the very process of cyclic existence (saṃsāra) would be contradicted.
Even the cessation of saṃsāra is not possible if the ālayavijñāna does not exist.
For the causes of saṃsāra are karma and the afflictions (kleśas),
and among these two, the afflictions are primary.
For it is through the predominance of the afflictions (*kleśa*) that karma becomes capable of projecting a future existence,
and not otherwise.
Therefore, the karma of those who have seen the truths does not project a future existence, because of the absence of the afflictions to be abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*).
Even karma that has projected a future existence does not result in rebirth due to the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*).

For instance, in the case of those who have become free from passion for the three realms, even karma that has projected a future existence lacks the power to bring about existence because of the absence of both karma and afflictions;
consequently, rebirth is not produced for them.
And thus, because they are predominant, the afflictions alone are the root of the progression of saṃsāra;
therefore, when these are abandoned, saṃsāra ceases, and not otherwise.
Furthermore, its abandonment is not tenable without the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna),
whether the affliction be abandoned while manifest or while in the state of a seed.
In that case, the claim that [an affliction] is abandoned when it has become manifest is certainly undesirable,
because at that time there is no path for its abandonment.
Nor is it abandoned while in the state of a seed.
For at that time, nothing other than the counteragent is admitted [as existing],
wherein the seed of the affliction might reside to be abandoned by that counteragent.
Or, if it is maintained that the seed of the affliction is attached to the very mind that is the counteragent, [then...]

For it is not logical that the antidote should be associated with the very seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Nor is the cessation of *saṃsāra* possible for those whose seeds of affliction have not been abandoned. Therefore, one must necessarily accept that the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is permeated by the primary and secondary afflictions coexisting with the other consciousnesses, through the process of depositing nourishment for their own seeds.

Furthermore, from that very same specific transformation of the continuum (*santatipariṇāmaviśeṣa*), when the activity of cultivation is attained according to one's strength, the afflictions (*kleśa*) and secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) arise.
Their seed, which is situated within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), is removed by the path that serves as the antidote to those afflictions and arises simultaneously with it.
Once that seed has been removed, the afflictions no longer arise based on that foundation; thus, the nirvana-element with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*) is attained.
And when the birth projected by prior karma ceases, because there is no further linking to another birth, that is the nirvāṇa-element without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).
For even though karma still exists, once the afflictions (*kleśa*) have been abandoned, it is incapable of producing renewed existence due to the absence of its auxiliary cause.
Therefore, it is precisely because the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) exists that there is the progression and cessation of saṃsāra.
It cannot be otherwise; therefore, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) must necessarily be accepted.
For what reason is it called "storehouse consciousness"?
Its status as storehouse consciousness consists in its being the repository of all seeds.
The term "depending on" (upādāya), which is taught at the end [of the verse], is connected to everything.
The state of being the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñānabhāva*) is the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñānatva*).
Furthermore, that is the ground for the application of the term "storehouse consciousness."
In this context, it is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it cognizes.

The designation of it as an agent is used merely for the sake of existence, in order to demonstrate that there is no cognizer distinct from it. Its nature as the storehouse of all seeds means it is the locus where the seeds of all defiled phenomena reside.

“Ālaya” and “sthāna” (abode) are synonyms. Alternatively, it is called *ālaya* because all phenomena adhere to and are bound within it as effects; or, it is called *ālaya* because it adheres to and is bound within all phenomena as their cause.
And it is based on its being the cause for the storehouse of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*).
"Personal existence" refers to name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); the personal existence is stored within this.
It is called the *ālaya* because it continues by means of that power;
its state is *ālayatā*.
It is the cause of the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*), because through the nourishment of its seeds, the personal existence is produced at the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhi*).
Based on its being the storehouse of the personal existence and its being the causal basis for the personal existence, it must be accepted as the *ālayavijñāna*.
Others, however, read it differently: "and by taking up the state of being the cause for the conceit of self and the storehouse.
The conceit that belongs to one who apprehends the storehouse-consciousness as a self is "the conceit of self" (*ātmamāna*).

The storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is so called because the conceit of self (*ātmamāna*) adheres to it by way of being its object; thus, it is the "abode of the conceit of self. Alternatively, it is called the "storehouse" (*ālaya*) because the conceit of self adheres to it by way of being its causal sign.
The remainder is as explained previously.
Regarding the phrase "and by means of its dependence on the body":
the word "and" (ca) has the sense of conjunction.
Here, "body" (kāya) refers to the physical frame together with the sense faculties.
For the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) exists pervading the entire body;
therefore, because its activity is bound to the body, it is "clinging to the body" (kāyālīna). Its state is "the nature of clinging to the body" (kāyālīnatā).
Based on that state of being merged with the body and having grasped it, its nature as the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is to be understood.
This is not called only the *ālayavijñāna*; rather, it is also called the *ādānavijñāna*. For what reason is it called the *ādānavijñāna*?
He states the reason for this: "because it takes up the appropriation of the body."
It is called the "appropriating consciousness" (*ādānavijñāna*) because by means of it, [the body] is appropriated;
it is well known that the appropriation of the body is by the mind (*citta*) and not by anything else.
And that which, caused by prior formative predispositions (*saṃskāra*), takes up existence in the state of the coagulation of semen and blood—
that very thing is intended as the appropriator of the body until death;
it is not the visual consciousnesses and so forth, nor the mental consciousness obtained subsequent to them.
This is because, from that point onward, they have as their cause the conditions of the currently functioning eye and other [senses];
nor is there any other mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) therein that has formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its cause,
since that [mental consciousness] is either wholesome or unwholesome.
For that which has formative forces (*saṃskāra*) as its cause is exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*),
because it is a maturation (*vipāka*); and a maturation is not something that is interrupted and then reconnected.
Like the eye and other [faculties],
no other [consciousness] is found that is exclusively of an indeterminate nature,
which could be postulated as the ripening-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Furthermore, because the six groups of consciousness function based on specific supports and because they function intermittently, it does not follow that all supports are appropriated.
For in this way, whichever consciousness functions by means of whichever support, only that [support] would be appropriated by that [consciousness].
The remaining [elements] would not be appropriated because they would be devoid of consciousness.
Furthermore, since visual consciousness and the others arise again and again after being interrupted, it would follow that their basis must be repeatedly appropriated.

Therefore, it is the *ālayavijñāna* alone that appropriates the body at the moment of rebirth (*pratisandhi*) and continues to function by means of the entire body as its support until death; thus, from the moment of the bond of rebirth onwards...
Because it takes up the body until death, it is called the "appropriating consciousness" (ādānavijñāna).
Primarily, the mind (*manas*) has the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as its object;
for the afflicted mind constantly takes the storehouse-consciousness as its object in the form of a self,
because it is associated with delusion, views, pride, and attachment that take the self as their object.
That [consciousness] is called "mind" (*manas*) because its nature is cogitation (*manyanā*) and it exists for a non-eternal duration;

it is specifically designated as "mind" because it is the consciousness that has just ceased immediately prior to the six groups of consciousness, such as visual consciousness and the rest. This is what is referred to as "mind."

That [designation] is for the purpose of establishing the basis (*āśraya*) of the sixth consciousness, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and not because it has the mode of activity (*ākāra*) of mentation (*manyana*);
therefore, it does not possess the nature of mind (*manas*) primarily.
And that [ignorance] is always associated with four afflictions: self-delusion (*ātmamoha*), self-view (*ātmadṛṣṭi*), self-pride (*ātmamāna*), and self-love (*ātmasneha*).
In this context, however, the mention of "self" does not refer to being associated with mere delusion;
rather, it refers to the delusion regarding a self.
The same should be stated up to self-love (*ātmasneha*).
Because of the inclusion of "and so forth" (*ādi*), it is always associated with the five universal factors (*sarvatraga*) such as contact (*sparśa*), attention (*manaskāra*), and the rest.

Since its nature is not well-known, and because mental factors (*caitta*) are also associated with other mental factors, he says "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) in order to determine its specific character.
"Of one kind" means it is of a defiled kind,
neither wholesome nor neutral,
because it is always associated with the four afflictions, beginning with self-delusion (*ātmamoha*).
And "continuity of the stream" means that it proceeds without interruption.
He begins the exception to this general rule: "Setting aside the states of Arhatship, the Noble Path, and the attainment of cessation.
It does not function in the state of Arhatship, because for an Arhat, all afflicted phenomena (*kliṣṭadharma*) of the three realms have been abandoned without remainder.
It does not function even during the stage of the noble path,
because the knowledge of ultimate reality is absolutely incompatible with the manifestation of the view of a self. Thereafter, its activity proceeds from the *ālayavijñāna*.
Because it has not been abandoned by one in training (*śaikṣa*),
it does not arise even during the state of the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
It should be understood that the attainment of cessation is more peaceful than the attainment of non-perception (*asañjñisamāpatti*) precisely because [the latter] is not free from that [defilement].
And here, it should be understood that the mind (manas) is explained by way of its etymology, its object, its association, and the time of its activity.
In what sense are they called "aggregates" (*skandha*), such as form and so forth? In the sense of a "heap. "Heap" and "aggregate" are synonyms.
This is what is meant: a heap of form is the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*);
likewise, up to a heap of consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*).

For it is stated in the Sūtra: "The aggregates of form and so forth are taught by way of the concise inclusion of those forms and so forth that are distinguished by differences of time, continuity, type, destiny, and location."

Whatever form there may be—whether past, future, or present; internal or external; gross or subtle; inferior or superior; far or near—all that, having been gathered together into a single whole, receives the designation "form-aggregate" (*rūpaskandha*). This applies likewise up to consciousness (*vijñāna*). These are distinguished by the division of time as "past, future, and present."
"Whether internal or external" refers to the distinction of the mental continuum (*santāna*);
for those that belong to one's own continuum are internal, while those other than those are external.
"Whether gross or subtle" refers to the distinction of their modes;
therein, the grossness and subtlety of form are relative:
that which possesses resistance is gross.
It is non-obstructive and subtle.
However, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—when arising based on the five sense faculties—are gross;
when mental, they are subtle.
"Whether inferior or superior" means they are distinguished by the difference in their destinies (*gati*);
for those comprised within an inferior destiny are inferior, while those comprised within a superior destiny are superior.
Or, "whether far or near" means they are distinguished by the difference in location (*deśa*).
As for feelings and the other aggregates, their relative distance or proximity is determined by way of their basis.
"Of form and so forth" means of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.

"By way of concise inclusion" means that for form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—which are differentiated by distinctions of time, continuum, mode, destiny, and location—there is a concise inclusion of each individually; this is "concise inclusion," and its state is "the nature of concise inclusion."
Based on this state of being a concise collection, the meaning of "aggregate" (*skandha*) in the Sūtra is understood as having the sense of a "heap.
For it has been said:
"All that form, whether past and so forth, when condensed into a single unit, comes to be designated by the term 'form-aggregate' (*rūpaskandha*)."
In this manner, it extends up to consciousness.
Thus, the five aggregates and the meaning of "aggregate" have been explained.
All conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) have been explained by way of their inclusion within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*),
and all phenomena (*dharma*), both conditioned and unconditioned, by way of their inclusion within the sense-bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*).
In this regard, immediately after the exposition of the aggregates, the sense-bases must be discussed.
And what is the meaning of "base" (*āyatana*)? To this he says: "the twelve bases. Which, then, are they?
They are the eye-base, the form-base, and so on, up to the mind-base and the phenomena-base.

"The exposition of the eye and so forth is as before" means that just as the eye and the other [faculties] were explained by way of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) in the analysis of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*),
they should likewise be explained here by way of their essential nature.
For it has been stated there: "The eye-faculty is a translucent matter (*rūpaprasāda*) that has as its object color derived from the four great elements.
In the same way, the ear and the other [faculties] are translucent matters consisting of form, having respectively sound, odor, taste, and the tangible as their objects.
And the explanation of the spheres (*āyatana*) of visible form, sound, odor, and taste is to be connected [to this] as before.
For it was previously stated that the objects of the eye are color, shape, and informative matter (*vijñapti-rūpa*).
The object of the ear is sound, which has as its cause the great elements (*mahābhūta*)—both appropriated, unappropriated, and both; and so forth.
These great elements, as well as that portion of the tangible (*spraṣṭavya*) which was mentioned, [constitute the objects of touch].
That, together with the great elements, is the sense-field of the tangible;
furthermore, it consists of smoothness and so forth.
The mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) is that which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
The eight consciousnesses constitute the aggregate of consciousness: the six evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
And the afflicted mind (kliṣṭa-manas);
however, in the formal arrangement of the sense-bases (āyatana), it is the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) alone that is called the mind-base (mana-āyatana).
Furthermore, it is of eight kinds: the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, non-informative matter (avijñapti), and the four unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta).
Among these, the aggregates of feeling, perception, and mental formations, as well as non-informative matter, have already been explained in the *Skandhavibhaṅga*.
Since the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) has not yet been mentioned, he asks with the desire to know its specific divisions: "What is the unconditioned?
That which does not have a nature dependent upon causes and conditions is called the unconditioned.
Space, non-analytical cessation, analytical cessation, and suchness—this is the demonstration of the divisions of the unconditioned.
"What is space? is the question asked for the purpose of understanding the essential nature of space.
"That which provides room for form" is the definition of its essential nature.
The same should be stated individually for non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*) and the others as well.
That location where resistant form (*sapratigha-rūpa*) is not obstructed is its space (*avakāśa*).
Therefore, space is so called because it provides room for material entities (*rūpin* bhāva).

Since it was mentioned immediately after space, the question "What is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*)? is asked immediately following its description, for the purpose of understanding its essential nature.
Here, *saṅkhyāna*, *tulana*, *vicaya*, and *prajñā* are synonymous.
The prefix *prati* has the sense of distribution (*vīpsā*).
This is what is meant: the individual discernment (*pratisaṅkhyāna*) of each of the Noble Truths, such as suffering and the rest, is *pratisaṅkhyā*;
the meaning is a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is neither analytical cessation nor non-analytical cessation.
What, then, is it?
It is the deficiency of conditions.
This is what is meant: the absolute non-arising of future dharmas due to the deficiency of conditions is "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
This explains the answer to the question: "What is that cessation which is not a dissociation (*visaṃyoga*)? and so forth.

For the word "cessation" (*nirodha*) here also applies to analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), the meditative attainment of cessation (*samāpatti-nirodha*), birth-cessation (*upapatti-nirodha*), and impermanence-cessation (*anityatā-nirodha*); therefore, in order to exclude analytical cessation, he says: "and not disjunction" (*na ca visaṃyoga*). For conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is established on the basis of the seeds existing and the fact that those future phenomena possess the nature of arising.

[Objection: Since that [cessation] is attained as the absolute non-arising of those [defilements] once their seeds have been extracted from their own basis by means of their antidote, it follows that this too would be a cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyānirodha*). Therefore, he says: "But that which is the absolute non-arising of the aggregates without an antidote to the defilements. This is what is meant: for even though the seeds of the wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral aggregates still exist, this is obtained without an antidote to the defilements; therefore, this is indeed cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*).
It is not non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
Thus, it is stated that both the *sopadhiśeṣa* and *nirupadhiśeṣa* nirvāṇa-realms are analytical cessations (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
Here, the "antidote to the afflictions" (*kleśapratipakṣa*) is intended to be the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*).
"Absolute non-arising":

the inclusion of the term "absolute" (atyanta) is for the purpose of excluding the cessation resulting from birth (*upapatti-nirodha*) and the cessation resulting from meditative attainment (*samāpatti-nirodha*);
for that [latter] is indeed a form of non-arising.
But it is not absolute,
because the arising of mind and mental factors occurs again;
"non-arising" refers to cessation through impermanence.
For the cessation through impermanence belongs to that which is present, and there is no non-arising of what is present;
rather, it belongs only to that which is future.

For example, when the visual consciousness is occupied with one type of form, those other objects and other types of forms that are capable of arising cannot be produced by the five groups of consciousness having them as their objects,
because of the absence of an immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) among the present [mental states].
Because past [dharmas] lack the condition of an object (ālambanapratyaya),
their analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyānirodha) is attained.
What is analytical cessation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*)? "Analysis" (*pratisaṅkhyā*) means *pratisaṅkhyāna*;
the meaning is a specific kind of wisdom (*prajñā*) comprised within the path of immediate succession (*ānantarya-mārga*).
"Cessation attained through analytical discernment" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) is so called by means of the elision of the middle term (*madhyapadalopa*).
As for the phrase "that which is cessation," since this would entail the consequence that all cessations [are meant], he says: "And that is dissociation" (*visaṃyoga*).
For in this way, it is distinguished from the remaining four types of cessation, because those [four] do not have the nature of dissociation (*visaṃyoga*).
He defines dissociation itself: "Furthermore, it is the absolute non-arising of the aggregates (*skandha*) by means of the antidote to the afflictions (*kleśa*)."
For this basis proceeds as permeated by the seeds of the afflictions of the three realms without remainder.
In that regard, whichever moment of the path serves as the antidote for whichever [affliction],
when that path arises, that moment of the basis is no longer able to produce the subsequent moment of the basis accompanied by the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned by it.
This is because of the presence of conditions that are incompatible with its arising.
Rather, it becomes the cause precisely for that which consists in the removal of the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned by it,
due to the existence of conditions conducive to its arising.

That very moment of the path is a discordant condition for the arising of another moment that is accompanied by the seeds of the afflictions to be abandoned by it; conversely, it should be understood as a concordant condition for the other [type of moment].

In this manner, up until the point when the antidote to the softest-of-soft category of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation has arisen, that basis (āśraya) consists precisely in the reversal of the seeds of all afflictions of the three realms—whether to be abandoned by seeing or by cultivation—without exception.
It becomes the cause for another moment.

Thus, when the seed of whichever affliction has been extracted due to the non-occurrence of its basis, the absolute non-arising of that affliction and of the factors associated with it is attained through the antidote to the affliction.
And that is called cessation through non-analytical discernment and dissociation.

Immediately after the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyānirodha*), suchness (*tathatā*) was mentioned; therefore, following that explanation, a question is asked for the sake of understanding suchness: "What is suchness?
Its definition is: "It is the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena, the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
Suchness is so called because it is non-alterability.
"Of phenomena" refers to form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
The "nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*) is their true state, their suchness, and the excellence of reality.
Since even the impermanence of the effects of phenomena and so forth exist as their true nature (*dharmatā*), he says: "the selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya*).
For that form by which phenomena become objects of cognition and verbal designation is their "self" (*ātman*).
Therefore, because they have emerged from the self and do not possess its intrinsic nature, they are "selfless" (*nirātman*);
the state of being so is the "selflessness of phenomena" (*dharmanairātmya*).
Furthermore, that is the emptiness of the imagined nature (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) of all entities.
But if this were to be investigated here, much would have to be said; therefore, enough with this digression, and we shall proceed with the subject at hand.

In what sense are they called "bases" (*āyatana*)? For the word "base" applies without distinction to the eye and so forth, which possess mutually distinct forms; therefore, it must apply to them by taking some common meaning as its basis. Since that [meaning] is not understood, the question is asked: "In what sense are they bases?"
"In the sense of being the gateway for the arrival of consciousness": "arrival" (āya) refers to coming;
it is the arising or the acquisition of self-existence of the consciousnesses.
The gateway for consciousness—that which is its cause, its reason, its motive—is the "gateway for consciousness.
What is meant by this is that the sense bases (*āyatana*) are so called in the sense of being the causes for the arising of consciousness.
But how is this to be understood?

From the etymological derivation (*nirvacana*): they are called *āyatanas* because they extend (*tanvanti*) and expand (*vistṛṇvanti*) the arrival (*āya*) of the mind (*citta*) and mental factors (*caitta*).
The meaning is that they establish the acquisition of self-nature (*ātmalābha*) through continuity.
Among these, the eye and visible forms are the gateway for the arrival of visual consciousness together with its associated mental factors.
In this way, up to the point that the mind and mental objects are the gateway for the arising of the mental consciousness together with its associated factors.

Immediately after the bases (*āyatana*), the elements (*dhātu*) must be explained both by way of their classification and their essential nature. Therefore, in order to show their classification, he says: "There are eighteen elements.

In order to demonstrate their essential nature, he says: "The eye element, the form element, the eye-consciousness element, and so on, up to the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.

For here, in the analysis of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), those five sense-faculties mentioned—the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body—and the five [objects], namely form, sound, odor, taste, and tangibles, are included as its objects.

In the establishment of the *āyatanas*, those same five faculties are called the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) and so forth, while their objects, form and so forth, are called the form-base (*rūpa-āyatana*) and so forth.

In the establishment of the *dhātus*, it is stated that those very things are the eye-element (*cakṣur-dhātu*) up to the body-element (*kāya-dhātu*), and the form-element (*rūpa-dhātu*) up to the tangible-element (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*). Therefore, he says: "In that regard, the elements of the eye and so forth, as well as the elements of form and so forth, are just as they were in the case of the bases."

The *dharmadhātu*, however, consists precisely of the *dharmāyatana*: the three aggregates beginning with sensation (*vedanā*), non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), and the four unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*).
In the systematic arrangement of the bases (*āyatana*), the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) alone constitutes the mind-base (*manāyatana*).
But it is not the case that, in the systematic arrangement of the elements (*dhātu*), the mind-base alone constitutes the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
What then? In the classification of the elements (*dhātu*), the mind-base (*mana-āyatana*) consists of the seven consciousness-elements (*citta-dhātu*).
Therefore, he says: "the six consciousness-elements," and so forth.
"Dependent upon the eye and so on" means dependent upon the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
"Having form and so forth as their objects" means having form, sound, odor, taste, tangibility, and mental phenomena as their objects.
"Representations" means consciousnesses.
In that regard, eye-consciousness—which has the eye as its support and form as its object—is the eye-consciousness-element (*cakṣurvijñānadhātu*).

In the same way, the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses—which have as their bases the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind, and which have as their objects sound, odor, taste, tangibles, and mental phenomena—are respectively the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousness elements (*vijñānadhātu*).
Furthermore, the mind element (*manodhātu*) does not exist apart from these six consciousnesses;
rather, those very six consciousness elements, having just ceased, are called the mind element.
But in that case, would there not result either seventeen elements or twelve,
because the mind-element (*manodhātu*) and the six consciousness-elements (*vijñānadhātu*) are mutually included within one another?
They do not so result.
Because the establishment of the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) is for the purpose of illustrating the basis (*āśraya*) of the sixth consciousness; "in this way" indicates the manner just mentioned;
and as for "that which is the aggregate of form" (*rūpaskandha*), the aggregate of form is said to consist of eleven substances (*dravya*).
In that regard, the five faculties beginning with the eye and the five objects beginning with visible form constitute ten bases (*āyatana*) in the classification of bases,

and ten elements (*dhātu*) in the classification of elements; furthermore, that which is called non-informative matter (*avijñapti*) constitutes a portion of the base of mental phenomena (*dharmāyatana*) and a portion of the element of mental phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
That which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is the sense-base of mind (*mana-āyatana*) and the seven elements of mind (*cittadhātu*),
namely, from the element of visual consciousness up to the element of mental consciousness.

Those other than the aggregate of form and the aggregate of consciousness— namely, the three aggregates called feeling, perception, and formations— as well as that portion of the aggregate of form called non-informative matter (*avijñapti*), [are included in the aggregate of formations].
These are the sphere of mental objects (dharmāyatana) and the constituent of phenomena (dharmadhātu), together with the unconditioned [factors] such as space and so forth.
In what sense are they called "elements" (*dhātu*)? This should be explained in detail according to the same sense as the "bases" (*āyatana*).
It is in the sense of maintaining their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) without activity.
They are called elements because they maintain their own specific characteristics while being devoid of activity.
For it has already been stated previously that activity is not possible for things that are momentary.

Since those very phenomena that were taught as the aggregates (skandhas) are again [taught] by way of the sense-bases (āyatana) and the elements (dhātu), he asks: "For what purpose is the teaching of the aggregates and so forth?
For all teachings of the Blessed Buddhas are purposeful, because they proceed for the benefit of sentient beings and serve as antidotes to the afflictions (kleśa).

Furthermore, the purpose here is not understood; namely, since those very same phenomena (dharmas) are taught again and again in various ways, one must state the purpose for why there is a teaching on the aggregates (skandhas) and so forth. Therefore, he says: "As an antidote to the threefold grasping at a self. In that regard, it is not understood what the threefold grasping at a self is, which teaching serves as the antidote to which, or which teaching corresponds to which. Therefore, he says: "The threefold grasping at a self is, in due order..."
There is the grasping at unity, the grasping at being an enjoyer, and the grasping at being an agent.
In that regard, they are respectively [applied] as follows: the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*) serves as the antidote to the grasping at unity;
the teaching on the sense bases (*āyatana*) serves as the antidote to the grasping at being an enjoyer; and...
The teaching on the elements (*dhātu*) is intended as an antidote to the grasping at agency.
For all proponents of a self (*ātmavādin*) maintain this position: "He who sees is the very same one who hears, smells, tastes, and touches."
In that regard, it is precisely he who feels who likewise intends, perceives, and cognizes.
For there exists no other entity whatsoever, distinct from the aggregates (skandhas), established as a single, unified form, which constitutes the self-nature of a sentient being.
Because its own nature and its activity are not perceived;
there exists no seer other than the eye.
For it is the eye itself—the uncommon cause and the support of the consciousness termed "seeing"—that is figuratively designated as the "seer."
