In this same way, it should be stated for each of the others, such as the ear and so forth.
Thus, because its nature consists in the experiencing of feeling, it feels;
because its nature consists in the grasping of signs, perception itself perceives.
"In this way, it should be stated everywhere that there is no other.
Therefore, the personal existence (*ātmabhāva*) of sentient beings does not consist of a single entity because it is composed of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*);
nor is there found here any single [entity] distinct from the aggregates.

When the grasping at unity has been overturned by the teaching on the aggregates (*skandha*), the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) that is preceded by that grasping at unity is likewise overturned. Therefore, the teaching on the aggregates serves as the antidote to the grasping at a self preceded by the grasping at unity.
Furthermore, the grasping at unity is referred to as "grasping at a self" by applying the metaphorical designation of the effect to the cause.

Furthermore, the grasping at a "consumer" held by all proponents [of self] is the notion that the self is that which experiences the desirable or undesirable fruit of wholesome or unwholesome karma— manifested as the sensations of pleasure and pain— as well as the objects such as forms and sounds.
As an antidote to this grasping at a self, there is the teaching on the sense bases (*āyatana*).
The enjoyment of the fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma, as well as of objects such as form and so forth, is perception.
He who performs that [perception] is the enjoyer of the fruits of karma and of objects such as form and so forth.
It is the sense bases alone, and nothing else, that constitute those six kinds of apprehension;
for this very reason, the eye and so forth, as well as visible forms and so forth, are called "bases" (āyatana) in the sense of being the gateways for the arising of consciousness.

Therefore, there is no other experiencer of the fruits of action and of objects apart from the eye and so forth; thus, the teaching on the sense bases (*āyatana*) serves as an antidote to the grasping at a subject who experiences.
Furthermore, the grasping at an agent is the notion that the self (*ātman*) is the doer of wholesome and unwholesome actions, as well as of acts such as jumping and clapping.

The teaching on the *dhātus* is for the purpose of counteracting this grasping at a self (*ātmagrāha*). For the *dhātus* have been taught in the sense of maintaining their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) without any [inherent] activity (*nirvyāpāra*).
Thus, a cause functions toward the arising of an effect by its mere existence (*sattāmātra*).
Furthermore, an effect depends upon its cause by its mere existence alone;
nor is there any action other than the essential natures of the effect and the cause,
as has already been established previously.
And how could there be an agent without action?
Therefore, the teaching on the elements (dhātu) is intended as an antidote to the grasping at agency.

[122] Now, for the purpose of assisting the discernment of phenomena (*dharmapravicaya*), the various types of those very phenomena that were previously taught as aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*) are considered.

Since, among these, the elements (*dhātu*) have been explained in detail through the differentiation of matter (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), the teaching on the types of contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava*) and so forth is easily understood; therefore, the investigation begins with the elements themselves.
The aggregates and sense-bases are not [the subject here], which is why he says: "Of the eighteen elements, how many are material? and so forth.
Matter (*rūpa*) is that which is subject to transformation (*rūpaṇa*); those which possess this are "material" (*rūpin*).
Alternatively, they are "material" because they possess matter as their basis or as what is based upon them, according to the case.
And there is no over-extension [of this definition] to the visual and other consciousnesses,
because the eyes and so forth serve as their supports, whereas those [consciousnesses] do not have them as their substratum.
As for those which have the nature of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*):
Furthermore, those ten elements are:
the eye element up to the body element,
and the form element up to the tangible object element.

Even though non-informative matter (avijñapti-rūpa) exists, it does not follow that the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) possesses materiality, because it lacks the materiality of a basis or that which is based upon it, because it is devoid of resistance (rūpaṇā), and because it is not included within the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha).
How many are formless? The remainder. Those which are the opposite of the formal.
Furthermore, those eight are the seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*) and the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*).
Regarding the question "how many are with demonstration? (*sanidarśana*), it is connected to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) because they are the subject under discussion.

"The single form-element" (rūpadhātu) means that this very designation of "this here" or "that there" is the demonstration (nidarśana). That which exists together with that is "with-demonstration" (sanidarśana).
Like that which possesses an object (*sālambana*). Elucidating this very point for the sake of illustration, he says: "by means of a demonstration of place" (*deśanidarśanena*).
That by which something is demonstrated in this or that particular place is a "demonstration of place."
Since only one element, the form-element (*rūpadhātu*), is included as being visible (*sanidarśana*), it is established that the remaining seventeen—
the five elements beginning with the eye, the four elements beginning with sound, the single dharma-element, and the seven mind-elements—
are non-visible (*anidarśana*).
How many are with resistance (*sapratigha*)?
Since eighteen elements (*dhātu*) are under discussion, this [question] applies to all of them.
Because non-informative matter (*avijñaptirūpa*) exists even within the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), it is designated as "material" (*rūpin*); thus, he says there are ten.
The term "material" (rūpin) is used for the purpose of excluding that which is formless (arūpi).
These, moreover, are the five sense-faculty elements (indriya-dhātu), such as the eye, and the five object-elements (viṣaya-dhātu), such as visible form;
"pratigha" means resistance (pratighāta).

They are called "with resistance" (*sapratigha*) because they exist together with resistance. Resistance is of three kinds, distinguished as resistance regarding the object-field (*viṣaya*), resistance regarding the objective support (*ālambana*), and resistance as obstruction (*āvaraṇa*). Here, however, demonstrating that "being with resistance" is intended solely in the sense of resistance as obstruction, he says: "wherein and that which is obstructed."

For obstruction by way of resistance (*āvaraṇapratighāta*) is the prevention of another's arising in one's own location. And thus, it is made known that both that by which the arising of another in its own location is prevented and that which is prevented are "possessing resistance" (*sapratigha*).

By this it is established that the ten material elements (rūpadhātu) are "with resistance" (sapratigha) due to the resistance of obstruction, insofar as they mutually obstruct the arising [of one another] in their own location; the remaining seven mental elements (cittadhātu) and the dharma-element (dharmadhātu) are "without resistance" (apratigha).
How many are with outflows (*sāsrava*)? The subject under discussion is "of the elements" (*dhātūnām*).
[The answer is: fifteen, and a portion of the last three.

The five sense-faculty elements beginning with the eye, the five object-elements beginning with visible form, and the five consciousness-elements beginning with visual consciousness—these fifteen are exclusively *sāsrava* (with outflows). Since the first three—the eye, visible form, and visual consciousness elements—also exist [as both *sāsrava* and *anāsrava*], he says "of the latter" (*paścimānām*). The latter three are the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mental-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*).
Of those as well, a portion— that is, a part— is with outflows (*sāsrava*),
but not all of them are with outflows like the eye and so forth.
Furthermore, that portion of theirs which does not have the nature of the truth of the path or the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) [is with outflows].
That itself is "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
They are called "with outflows" because they exist together with the outflows.
For this very reason, it is said: "because the afflictions arise within them."
Because afflictions arise with respect to those [objects],
they are called "with outflows" (*sāsrava*).
Since the consciousnesses of the eye and so forth are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*), how can there be the arising of afflictions with respect to forms and other objects?
It is not said that afflictions arise with respect to forms and so forth only together with the visual consciousness and the others;
rather, the arising of afflictions with respect to forms and so forth is stated by way of their being objects of direct perception.
For it is thus: depending on the eye and depending on forms, visual consciousness arises.
Forms experienced by visual consciousness are conceptualized by mental consciousness, and from such conceptualization, afflictions arise;
the same should be stated for the remaining [senses] as well.
How many are untainted (*anāsrava*)? A portion of the last three:

that part of the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*), and the mind-consciousness-element (*manovijñānadhātu*) which is comprised within the truth of the path (*mārgasatya*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Thus, it is "without outflows."
How many are associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*)? This is connected with the phrase "of the eighteen elements.
The five objects, beginning with form (*rūpa*), are called "desires" (*kāma*) because they are desired.
The realm characterized primarily by that is the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Those things associated with it are called "associated with desire" (*kāmapratisaṃyukta*).
Alternatively, although it should have been stated as "associated with the desire realm" (*kāmadhātupratisaṃyukta*), they are called "associated with desire" through the elision of the word *dhātu*.
The meaning is that those things associated with desire (*kāma*), comprised within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), and having the nature of the desire realm are [the objects of the first dhyāna].
Likewise, wherever there is the active manifestation of craving for desire (*kāmatṛṣṇā*),
all that is comprised within the desire realm.
Furthermore, all these consist of the six sense-faculty elements, the six object-elements, and the six consciousness-elements.
How many are associated with form? Fourteen.
Among them, six are the elements of the faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind.
The four sense-object elements and the four consciousness elements that have them as their objects— these fourteen are associated with the realm of form (rūpadhātu).
What, then, is the reason that odors and tastes, as well as their corresponding consciousnesses, do not exist in the realm of form?
For smell and taste are exclusively of the nature of the food consisting of mouthfuls (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*),
and not of the nature of the foods of contact or sensation (*sparśavedanāhāra*).
Furthermore, those who are free from desire for the food consisting of mouthfuls are reborn in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Wherever those who are free from passion are reborn, there is the absence of that [passion] for them;
just as, for example, there is the absence of the eye and other faculties in those free from passion for the realm of form when they attain the formless realm.
And because of the absence of their objects, there is also the absence of the consciousnesses of odor and taste.
How many are associated with the formless realm? The last three:
the mind element, the mental-object element, and the mind-consciousness element.
For those who are free from passion for form are born in the formless realm;
therefore, there the ten elements whose intrinsic nature is form, as well as the five consciousness-elements which have them as their basis and objects, do not exist.
How many are non-bound?
Those which are untainted (anāsrava),
and those which are not taken as objects by craving for the realms of desire, form, or formlessness.
Because they are dissociated from the three realms, they are non-bound.
Those which have the nature of the truth of the path and the unconditioned—namely, the mind-element, the phenomena-element, and the mind-consciousness-element—are untainted (*anāsrava*).
How many are wholesome, how many are unwholesome, and how many are indeterminate?
This is connected to "of the eighteen elements" because that is the subject under discussion. In this context, *kuśala* means "slipped away from what is contemptible";
the meaning is "gone."
Alternatively, *kuśa* is a synonym for wisdom (*prajñā*).
The root *lā* means "to take.
Thus, those who are embraced by wisdom or who embrace wisdom are "skillful" (*kuśala*).
They are called *kuśas* because they lie down with a contemptible form;
they are cutters and piercers.
The root *lā* means "to take."
He who takes up kusha grass while avoiding cutting or piercing is called "skillful" (kuśala);
likewise, any other person who deserves praise for a particular action [is so called].
That is called wholesome therein;
by this, the unwholesome is explained.
They are indeterminate because they are not defined as being either wholesome or unwholesome.

"Ten are of three kinds"—that is, they are wholesome (*kuśala*), unwholesome (*akuśala*), and neutral (*avyākṛta*). However, it is not yet known which ten among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) these are; therefore, he says: "The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*), as well as the form, sound, and mental-object elements.
In this context, the wholesomeness or unwholesomeness of the mind-elements is determined by their association (*samprayoga*).
Not from themselves,
nor from the roots of the wholesome and unwholesome.
In that regard, seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) associated with non-attachment, non-hatred, and non-delusion are wholesome.
Those associated with greed, hatred, and delusion are unwholesome;
others are indeterminate.
The elements of visible form and sound, when originated by a wholesome or unwholesome mind, are themselves wholesome or unwholesome, as they are comprised within bodily and vocal intimation.
Therefore, the other two [realms] are indeterminate.

The dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) is wholesome when it has as its intrinsic nature, is associated with, or is originated by non-attachment and so forth; it is unwholesome when it has as its intrinsic nature, is associated with, or is originated by attachment and so forth; and it is also [indeterminate as] analytical cessation (pratisaṅkhyānirodha) and suchness (tathatā).
Other than those, the rest are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Eight are indeterminate: odor, taste, and tangibility, as well as the five beginning with the eye.
For these are exclusively indeterminate because, by virtue of their ultimate nature, their association, and their origination, they lack the quality of being either wholesome or unwholesome.
How many are internal?
This is connected with "of the eighteen elements";
[the answer is] twelve.
But as for those that are not specified—namely, which twelve?—he says: "excluding the elements of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
The remaining six sense-faculty elements and the six consciousness elements—these twelve are internal.
How many elements are external? Six.
But since they are not yet understood, he says: "those which were set aside."
These should be understood as external.
And which ones are set aside?
The elements of form, sound, odor, taste, tangible objects, and mental phenomena.
"Adhyātma" means "with reference to the self" (adhy-ātmānam). That which is with reference to the self is precisely "internal" (ādhyātmika).
If the self does not exist, how can there be anything internal or external?
For without ethical discipline (*śīla*), training in higher ethical discipline (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*) is not possible.
Because it is dependent upon the conceit of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*), the mind is metaphorically designated as the "self" (*ātman*);
for that which is the basis of the conceit of "I" is what is called the "self" by those who propound a self-theory.
For they have understood the *ahaṅkāra* as a quality of the self (*ātman*) and as having the self as its object;
and since there is no self distinct from that [mind], the *ahaṅkāra* is based upon the mind.
It is called the "self" (*ātman*) because the conceit of "I" (*ahaṃmāna*) is deposited within it.
Since the mind alone is the basis for mental factors (*caitta*), the mind itself is metaphorically designated as the "self.
But how is it understood that the mind is intended here as the self?
For it was said by the Blessed One: "By means of a well-tamed self, the wise person attains heaven."
And elsewhere, the taming of the mind has been taught: "The taming of the mind is good;
a tamed mind brings happiness.
For here, it is stated that the taming of the mind is simply the mind itself being tamed, which brings happiness.
Therefore, it is understood that even here, when it is said, "By means of a well-tamed self, the wise man attains heaven," it is the mind (*citta*) alone that is intended.
Consequently, because the mind—which has become the self—is proximate by virtue of being their basis, the eye and other [faculties] are internal;
whereas form and other [objects], by virtue of being objective domains, are external.

If that were so, then the six consciousness-elements would not qualify as internal; for they do not become the support of the mind (*citta*) until they have attained the status of the mind-element (*manodhātu*).
At whatever time they become those [supports], they do not transcend their defining characteristic.
The subject under discussion is: "How many elements have an object? To this he says: "Seven.
Since it is not known which seven, he says: "The mind-elements."
Are these alone possessed of an object?
No;
rather, it is also a portion of the dharma-element (dharmadhātu).
The word "ca" (and) signifies a conjunction: the seven mental elements (*cittadhātu*) and a portion of the dharma-element (*dharmadhātu*) possess an object (*sālambana*).
They are called "possessing an object" because they have an object (*ālambana*).
"Object" (*viṣaya*), "sphere" (*gocara*), and "object of cognition" (*ālambana*) are synonyms.

The seven mind-elements (*cittadhātu*)— namely, the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, mental consciousness elements, and the mind-element (*manodhātu*)— as well as that portion of the phenomena-element (*dharmadhātu*) which has the nature of mental factors (*caitasika*).
How many are without an object?
The remaining ones.
These, moreover, are ten: the five sense-faculty elements, beginning with the eye, and the five object-elements, beginning with visible form.
And it is a portion of the dharma-sphere (dharmadhātu) which does not have the nature of a mental factor (caitasika).
How many are conceptual?
This refers to the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).
They are the mind element (*manodhātu*), the mental consciousness element (*manovijñānadhātu*), and that portion of the phenomena element (*dharmadhātu*) which is associated [with the mind].
For these two are associated with the conceptualizations of investigation and recollection;
they alone are conceptual, not the other two.
Because of the lack of association with those two,
even that portion of the dharma-element which is associated [is not included], while the other is not.
Among these, conceptualization as recollection (*anusmaraṇa-vikalpa*) is simply mindfulness (*smṛti*), which is mental, characterized by the non-forgetting of a previously experienced object.

Conceptualization as investigation (*abhirūpaṇā-vikalpa*) is a specific form of wisdom (*prajñā*) or volition (*cetanā*), characterized by the inferential deliberation regarding objects of the three times that are not present to the senses, thinking "it is thus" or "it is not thus.
As it is said in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*: "What is conceptualization as recollection?"

What is the conceptualization of investigation (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of inferential reasoning regarding things that are not present to the senses, whether they belong to the past, the future, or the present. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of previously experienced formations (*anubhūta-pūrva-saṃskāra-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of recollection. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the present (*pratyutpanna-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of direct perception of objects currently present before one. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the future (*anāgata-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of anticipation regarding things yet to come. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the past (*atīta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of memory regarding things already passed. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the unmanifested (*avyākṛta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of deliberation regarding things that have not been manifested. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the manifested (*vyākṛta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of determination regarding things that have been manifested. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the indeterminate (*aniyata-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of uncertainty regarding things that are not fixed. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the determinate (*niyata-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of certainty regarding things that are fixed. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the inferior (*hīna-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of disparagement regarding inferior things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the superior (*praṇīta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of praise regarding superior things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the beautiful (*śubha-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of attachment regarding beautiful things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the ugly (*aśubha-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of aversion regarding ugly things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the self (*ātma-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of grasping at a self regarding what is not-self. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of non-self (*anātma-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of discernment regarding the absence of a self. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of permanence (*nitya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of eternalism regarding what is impermanent. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of impermanence (*anitya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of understanding regarding the nature of impermanence. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of suffering (*duḥkha-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of distress regarding what is suffering. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of happiness (*sukha-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of craving regarding what is happiness. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of peace (*śānta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of tranquility regarding what is peaceful. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of non-peace (*aśānta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of agitation regarding what is not peaceful. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of emptiness (*śūnya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of insight into the absence of a self and what belongs to a self. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of non-emptiness (*aśūnya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of grasping at a self and what belongs to a self. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of existence (*bhava-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of clinging to the cycle of existence. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of non-existence (*vibhava-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of seeking liberation through annihilation. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of renunciation (*naiṣkramya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of turning away from worldly desires. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of non-renunciation (*anaiṣkramya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of indulgence in worldly desires. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the outflow-free (*anāsrava-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the with-outflows (*sāsrava-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the path leading to the increase of suffering. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of arising and ceasing. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the cessation of arising and ceasing. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the worldly (*laukika-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of attachment to the world. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the supramundane (*lokottara-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of detachment from the world. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the common (*sāmānya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of similarity among different things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the specific (*viśeṣa-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of distinction among similar things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the name (*nāma-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of designating things by means of names. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the referent (*vastu-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of apprehending the actual entities of things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the sign (*nimitta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of grasping the characteristics of things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the signless (*animitta-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the non-grasping of characteristics. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of defining the essential marks of things. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the characteristicless (*alakṣaṇa-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the non-defining of essential marks. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the truth (*satya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of conviction in the Four Noble Truths. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the untruth (*asatya-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of denial of the Four Noble Truths. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the cause (*hetu-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of understanding the origin of suffering. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the non-cause (*ahetu-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the view of no-cause. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the fruit (*phala-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of understanding the cessation of suffering. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the non-fruit (*aphala-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the view of no-result. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the path (*mārga-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of practicing the way to cessation. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the non-path (*amārga-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of following a wrong path. What is the conceptualization of the aspect of the right (*samyak-ākāra*)? It is the conceptualization that takes the form of the Eightfold Noble Path. It is established that the remaining [elements] are non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*).
These, moreover, are the fifteen elements and a portion of the dharma-element;
for these are exclusively non-conceptual.
Among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), how many are appropriated (*upātta*)?
Five are internal;
these, moreover, are the elements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
For these are indeed appropriated.
But are they not taught elsewhere as being of two kinds? True, they are so taught.
For in that context, the past and future are said to be non-appropriated (*anupātta*),
yet they do not exist at all;
and it is not logical for that which does not exist to be either appropriated or non-appropriated.
However, the present [elements], such as the eye and so forth, are indeed appropriated because they are presided over by their own existence and are grasped by the mind and mental factors;
they are not unappropriated.
Are the five [senses] beginning with the eye alone appropriated?
No;
rather, it is a portion of four.
To the question "Of which four?", he says: "Of visible form, taste, odor, and the tangible."
In that regard, those elements of form, odor, taste, and tangibility which exist inseparably from the sense faculties are appropriated, just like the sense faculties themselves;
others are unappropriated.
For example, [this refers to] hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—excluding the roots—as well as excrement, urine, saliva, nasal mucus, blood, and so forth, and also to earth, water, and the like.
What is the meaning of "appropriated" (*upātta*)? It is that which is grasped by the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) by way of being their basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
Because they mutually conform to one another through benefit and injury,
that which is called "sentient" in the world [is so designated].
How many are non-appropriated?
The remaining nine and a portion of four;
those other than the appropriated are the "remaining" ones.

Therefore, it consists of the seven mental elements (cittadhātu), the dharma-element (dharmadhātu), the sound-element (śabdadhātu), and a portion of four [elements], namely form, odor, taste, and touch. Furthermore, this refers to that which exists in hair, body hair, and so forth— excluding the roots— while setting aside the portion that exists inseparable from the sense faculties.
How many are homogeneous?
This refers back to the context of "among the eighteen elements.
Those [first] five are internal.
The twelve internal [elements] have been mentioned;
it is not known which among them are the five. Therefore, he says: "the material ones. These, moreover, are the elements of the eye, ear, nose, tongue, and body.
It is not known whose they are similar to (sabhāga), nor in what manner they are similar.
Therefore he says: "having taken up the state of generality with respect to their own cognitions.
In this context, the "own cognition" of the eye is visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*).
By means of that own cognition, the eye is similar to its own object, which is visible form (*rūpa*).
Because both are equally conducive to the arising of visual consciousness, they are alike.
Taking this commonality as the basis—that is, by virtue of it— the eye is said to be "functioning" (sabhāga) with respect to its own object, visible form.
In the same way, the functioning of the ear and the other [faculties] with respect to their own objects should also be explained.
This is what is meant: those [faculties] such as the eye which are presided over by their own respective cognitions are "homogeneous" (sabhāga).
Those very same [faculties], such as the eye and so forth, when devoid of their own respective consciousnesses, are "partially homogeneous" (*tatsabhāga*).
For what purpose, then, are they called "partially homogeneous"? It is on account of their commonality with their own kind (*svajātisāmānyatām upādāya*).

The eye and other [faculties] that are devoid of their own consciousness are called "partially similar" (*tatsabhāga*) because they are similar to those eyes and so forth that are "functioning" (*sabhāga*), being equal to them by way of the genus of the eye and so forth;

for since these are not common [to all], whatever are functioning or partially similar for one person are likewise so for all sentient beings, and thus their status as functioning or partially similar is certain.

However, since the state of being "homogeneous" (sabhāga) or "partially homogeneous" (tatsabhāga) applies to form and the other [sensory objects] only within each individual continuum, it is not fixed; and since there is no functional activity (kāritra) other than consciousness itself, the state of being homogeneous or partially homogeneous is not predicated of the others.
The *Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā* is completed.
This is the work of the teacher Sthiramati.

"Of those phenomena which arise from causes, the Tathāgata has declared their cause, as well as their cessation; such is the teaching of the Great Śramaṇa. This is the religious gift of the Śākya bhikṣu Vibhūticandra, a follower of the supreme Mahāyāna.

Whatever merit there is herein, may it, placing the preceptors, teachers, mother, and father foremost, result in the attainment of the fruit of unsurpassed knowledge for the entire mass of sentient beings. [Dated] in the reign of Govindapāla, in the year, on the day of Vaiśākha.
